Industry News: Lafayette 148’s Emily Smith on 30 Years in Fashion and Finding Her Uniform

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between.
  • I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher.
  • At a certain point, I discovered Donna Karan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Lafayette 148 creative director Emily Smith as the New York-based fashion house celebrates its 30th anniversary. Smith has spent more than two decades at the helm of the brand, working her way up from a part-time freelancer to creative lead. But her fashion ambitions began long before she arrived in New York. Growing up in Atlanta, she ran her own neighborhood art camp before discovering designers like Donna Karan and realizing fashion could be a career. Now, Smith is celebrating the women who have shaped Lafayette 148 through its “Uniform” campaign, which highlights accomplished New Yorkers and their individual approaches to personal style. Below, Smith reflects on her unconventional start, why she’s stayed at the tech giant for over 20 years, and the career advice she wishes she’d followed sooner.

I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher. It was basically babysitting all the neighborhood kids, but I created a flyer, got paid for it, and did the whole thing. I started in second grade, and we did it every year for about eight years. I even started hiring people so we could have two classes going at once. We had swimming lessons. The local news even came and did a segment on it. I loved decorating my classroom and setting everything up. My parents were so nice to give me the garage and basement to do it all. Not necessarily an official job, but my first money-making moment.

I was a bagger at Kroger. It just was not for me.

I was always creative growing up. At a certain point, I discovered Donna Karan. It’s kind of crazy when you see somebody doing something and suddenly realize, Oh, that’s a career. I can do that. I became obsessed with everything in the ’90s, all the Latest York fashion at the time. That was when I decided I wanted to pursue it. When college applications came around, my mom really encouraged me to go to art school. I started in fashion, and that became my focus. Growing up in Atlanta, I wasn’t necessarily surrounded by a massive fashion community. But my dad’s office was across the street from the art museum at one point, and I remember going there and having that exposure. My mom was always crafty and creative, too. She really encouraged us to be who we were.

There’s a language creative people have that’s a little different from the way business people communicate. When I went to art school, I felt like I’d found my people. It wasn’t just fashion people. It was photographers, fine artists, and all these different kinds of creatives. Being around people who thought about things differently was really inspiring. Even today, I thrive around people who have creative insight. There’s always a little more depth to the way they see things.

Industry observers note that I interned at Bill Blass for about six months. I moved to Newly introduced York in July 2001, and we had our fashion show on September 10. I remember Marc Jacobs had his show that day, too, and everybody was celebrating. People were saying, “Just come a little late to work tomorrow.” And then, obviously, September 11 happened. A week later, the entire team was let go, from the top down. What I learned from that experience was the fragility of everything. Don’t take anything for granted. Anything can come and go in a moment. But I also worked with Lars Nilsson and Hervé Pierre Braillard, who were just the kindest people. This industry has a little bit of everything, but I loved that they led with kindness, even when they were under so much pressure. As an intern, I was literally carrying ironing boards down the street and doing a sketch here or there. It was very much about doing whatever needed to be done.

Sources indicate that after my internship, I had a brief stint of freelancing. Those were some long months. I remember coming home from one job and my roommates asking how my day was. I remarked, “Well, I was putting pigs on socks.” I knew I wouldn’t be going back. Freelancing is hard. It’s a grind, but you meet a lot of great people. I actually made some really good contacts during that time. I eventually met Deirdre [Quinn], Lafayette 148’s founder. She met with me on a Saturday, which I thought was incredible. I was really just looking for advice. I wasn’t looking for a job, and I didn’t even know much about the brand. It was only five years old. She was so kind, full of knowledge, and passionate. After I spent a year freelancing and meeting people who seemed so over the industry, her enthusiasm reminded me why I wanted to do this in the first place. She offered me a part-time freelance position, and the rest is history.

In the beginning, security was really notable to me. The idea of losing a job and having to pay rent was scary, so that was definitely part of it initially. But really, it was the growth. Within a couple of years, they were sending me to the factory. It was a small, tight-knit firm, so I was able to wear a lot of different hats. I had a mentor named Barbara Gast who was traveling back and forth from Italy, and I was learning so much from her. I’d compare notes with friends in the industry and realize how much hands-on experience I was getting. I understood the value of that and really loved being so close to the product. It never got boring. And whenever things did get slightly boring, I’d ask, “Okay, what’s next?” And there was always something. It’s such an entrepreneurial place that you can almost create your next opportunity. That’s what made it so exciting.

It has been revealed that I think if you asked Deirdre, she’d have a different answer because she has her own experience of building the company. For me, it’s about having started at a company that was really a factory and being part of the journey of building its identity and what it stands for. I was the kid running up and down the factory floors collecting samples. That hustle and bustle was so innate to who the brand was. To me, it was really exciting to build more of a brand story around that. Thirty years later, we’re still celebrating those roots and making sure we haven’t strayed too far from them, while continuing to evolve. Being part of that journey has been really exciting.

The constant has always been this idea of an accomplished woman. She’s always been at the forefront of who we’re designing for. At the time, it was the career woman. But now, what does that even mean anymore? What does that look like? There are so many different versions of that woman and so many different ways people dress. At the heart of it, she’s a woman who knows what she wants. She’s busy and has a really full life, whether she’s starting her career or ending it. They can all find something in the clothes.

In a recent development, for us, it was about choosing people who inspire us. Number one, they had to be Fresh York women. That was the base. We wanted women who make us want to be better ourselves. From someone like Deborah Berke, the architect, to women who have built incredible careers in other fields, it’s important to shine a light on them. I think back to when I was a kid and how much you need that kind of inspiration. Even at a certain stage in your career, when you’re wondering what the point is, it’s nice to have people who inspire you. These are women who have really built something for themselves, and I think that’s worth celebrating.

Sophie de Rakoff said something during the project that I really liked, and I’m going to steal it: “Dressing with intention.” When you know yourself, you know what works on you. It’s no longer about dressing to impress. There’s a confidence in knowing what works for you and making it work. We’re all so busy. Who has time to overthink getting dressed? You know what works, and you build a system around that. You’re able to create a wardrobe that really works for you. Everybody has a different definition of a uniform, and that was the whole point of the project.

Recent findings suggest that when I first started in the industry, I was a total hippie. I was making my own clothes, and they were terrible. Absolutely falling apart. It was what it was. I think part of the change comes from not having as much time as you did when you were younger. But it’s also about simplicity and comfort. I know that if I’m going to be on the floor pinning something but also have to give a presentation, there are certain pieces that work for both. I can be comfortable and still feel appropriately dressed. I’ve found a handful of things that work for me, and I don’t have to think too much about them anymore. A crisp, oversize white cotton button-down is half my closet. I also love a soft skirt and a big chunky sweater. Those are the pieces I always go back to and interchange depending on the day. I even wear sweaters in the summer. It’s cold in the Navy Yard!

According to recent reports, our pants fit incredibly well. The moment somebody gets into our pants, they’ll love us forever. Then it’s the jacket and the white shirt. Those three things are our gateway pieces, and everything else follows. You need a good blazer and a good leather piece, too. Once you find those foundational pieces that really work for you, everything else becomes easier.

It has been revealed that I really want to see more women in our clothes. It’s not just about growing the business. It makes me happy when I see people put on our clothes and feel really good. We work so hard to make sure things fit the way a woman wants them to fit. I just want more people to enjoy that.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is equally about food and football in my house, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing was a no-brainer creation for me. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

It has been revealed that how we’re making the beer cheese:A high-quality cheddar and flavorful beer are both key to making beer cheese sing. Make sure to choose a beer you love, since you’ll definitely taste it in the finished stuffing. I recommend a lager or an amber ale, since hoppier beers like IPAs can be too assertive in the larger context of a stuffing. When it comes to cheese, I love extra-sharp cheddar here, but you could also try a milder cheddar if you like.

Sources indicate that to achieve a glossy, silky texture, this beer cheese harnesses the dual powers of cornstarch and evaporated milk. Together with the lager, they form a smooth, stable base that helps keep the sauce smooth and emulsified, even when it’s heated to bubbling in the oven.

Make ahead & storage:I don’t recommend assembling this stuffing in advance, but if you want to work ahead, you can make the beer cheese up to 2 days before. Let it cool completely, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator. When you’re ready to assemble, reheat it slowly on low heat before layering it with the bread.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can swiftly morph into delicious meals. This month, it’s all about boxed stuffing.

Industry observers note that few Thanksgiving dishes inspire as many strong opinions as stuffing-slash-dressing. In a baking dish or the bird itself? Sourdough or white bread? Fresh herbs or dried? Sausage or nah? There are the purists, who insist on drying their own bread, chopping aromatics, and seasoning everything from scratch. Then there are the Stove Top loyalists, who grew up on that unmistakable red box and remain fiercely faithful. Site director Rachel Tepper Paley is firmly in the latter camp. “My late father considered boxed Stove Top the Platonic ideal of stuffing, so I grew up with the uber-savory stuff on every Thanksgiving table,” she says. “We continue to serve it every year in his honor.”.

According to recent reports, and then there’s a particularly resourceful subset of boxed-stuffing devotees: the maximalists who see the box as a pantry staple, not just a holiday shortcut. Our editors happen to be among them. Read on for all the ways they’re thinking outside the box.

The first time I tried my colleague Jesse Szewczyk’s Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet in the Test Kitchen, I immediately started plotting all the occasions I could make it: Friendsgiving, a random Tuesday, football Sunday, date night. Its deliciousness caught me off guard. Jesse sears chicken thighs until golden and crisp, then uses the schmaltzy drippings (a.k.a. liquid gold) to season the boxed stuffing. Dotted with sweet-tart cranberry gems, then baked with the chicken nestled back in, it’s basically Thanksgiving in one pan—and a recipe I proposal to make well beyond November. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

In a recent development, when I find myself with instant stuffing, I like to make a baked eggs situation. I’ll make the stuffing according to the box’s directions in a shallow oven-proof skillet. With the heat on (so the stuffing continues to crisp), I’ll toss in some greens like kale or spinach until they’re just barely wilted. Then I’ll use a spatula to make a couple divots throughout and crack an egg into each. From there, I’ll pop the skillet into a 375° oven and bake until the whites are set, about 15 minutes. A drizzle of green hot sauce and some salty feta crumble or sliced avocado, and I’m ready to eat. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor.

Sources indicate that the way I see it, boxed stuffing mix is really close to a box of well-seasoned breadcrumbs. So why not use it as a savory panade that transforms lean ground turkey into tender meatballs? Senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk called this sheet-pan dinner Turkey and Stuffing Meatballs, but it honestly delivers all the flavors of Thanksgiving in one simple meal. You’ve got creamy baby Yukon gold potatoes and snappy green beans, plus a dipping sauce made from another autumn pantry staple, canned cranberry sauce, with lemon and honey to serve alongside. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

According to recent reports, as a person who works in food media, I end up with my fair share of “what can I do with this?” ingredients. So while I firmly believe that no Thanksgiving dressing matters as much as my classic cornbread-and-biscuit version, I am no stranger to boxed stuffing. Frequently, it becomes a crust for baked fish. I’ve used Anna Stockwell’s easy no-recipe-required crispy fish method dozens of times since it first published, and it never disappoints. Best of all, you can use whatever bits and bobs you have lying around to build out the meal, and it’s relatively hands-off. Wins all around. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

For cozy season, there is nothing more comforting than carbs on carbs. I’ve always loved pasta with breadcrumbs (every which way), but leave it to senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk to make that classic combo even better: In this recipe, instead of using plain breadcrumbs or Italian seasoned ones, he swaps in stuffing mix blitzed in the food processor. Brilliant. It’s a highly flavorful topping for pasta with sausage and kale, a total delight for a cold night. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Sources indicate that slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

According to recent reports, A paloma is a classic summer cocktail in my rotation, but I still want an excuse to enjoy it throughout the colder-weather months. Enter: the cranberry paloma. Just like a classic paloma, this version is made with a base of tequila and grapefruit. But it gets a boost of sweetness and tartness with the addition of cranberry juice cocktail. This sweetened cranberry-based beverage replaces the need for sugary sodas or simple syrup. Bonus: It adds a gorgeous red hue to your glass, perfect for the holiday season.

It has been revealed that reposado tequila:The type of tequila you use is ultimately up to you, but I recommend either reposado or blanco tequila. Reposado tequila is aged for up to a year, typically in oak barrels, and takes on a warm sweetness with notes of vanilla and caramel. It’s a great choice for cocktails (especially when grapefruit is involved) because the smoothness balances out the tart and bright citrus.

Blanco tequila:Blanco tequila, on the other hand, is for people who want to double down on the brightness. It’s barely aged, if aged at all, so it retains the sharp, vegetal flavor of the agave plant. This recipe works well with either option, so it all comes down to personal preference and what you already have on your bar cart.

According to recent reports, CARRANCA draws on the eponymous sculptures, anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figures traditionally believed to ward off evil spirits, also associated with Afro-Brazilian religious traditions such as Candomblé. The project references Exu, the orisha who mediates between the material and spiritual worlds and is associated with movement and the creation of possibilities. Inspired by ancient Egyptian and Yoruba cultures, the carrancas’ physiognomy blends human and animal traits, evoking pre-dynastic Egyptian deities.

According to recent reports, the palette of black, red, indigo, and white references these traditions and Brazilian popular representations of Exu. Using Afro-surrealism as a conceptual framework, the series visually narrates Urias’ eponymous album, with each photograph corresponding to a track. The project explores transcorporeality and how reclaiming divine and ancestral figures can become a means of liberation from Eurocentric identity norms.

Creative Director, Art Director and Stylist: OdePhotography: MaltoniSet Design: Jean LabancaHair and Makeup: Ivan BarriaUrias’ Hair: Rafaella SchlinUrias’ Makeup: Camila AnacNail Artist: CyshimiProduction: BELTRAME+Post-Production: Studio Bruno RezendeCast: Fina Cadjancu, Akin Henrias and Marcinha do Corintho.

Ode (b. 1998) is a Brazilian multidisciplinary artist working across filmmaking, creative direction, styling, writing, and curatorial practice. Her work explores self-representation as a means of challenging Eurocentric notions of identity through transcorporeality, Afro-Brazilian spirituality, memory, and transformation. Her photobooks and films, including A Rose and A Prayer (2022), Divina (2022), and CARRANCA (2025), bring human figures, deities, and Afro-surrealist narratives into dialogue. Her work has been exhibited at MEP, Instituto Moreira Salles, Lafayette Anticipations, ICA London, Photo London, and SP-Arte. She founded the platform Dúdús (2016–2019) and has curated exhibitions dedicated to Afro-diasporic art. Her work has been featured in Vogue, Dazed, ArtReview, and Harper’s Bazaar, and she has collaborated with Comme des Garçons, Jean Paul Gaultier, and COLORSxSTUDIOS.

The pair are perfectly matched: Casio watches are known for being beautifully functional and understated—adjectives that fit APC’s spartan aesthetic too.

It has been revealed that the first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch. That release stripped back a lot of the original’s markings and added the APC logo on the dial. This time around, it's the AQ-240 getting a makeover. The case is squarer than the rectangular A1000, and while there’s a narrow window for a digital display, the watch maintains the traditional analog format with hands and hour markers. Here, you get the best of both worlds. The watch is sold out on APC's website but still available through Casio, so act fast if you want one. The silver variant is $110, and the gold goes for $135.

In a recent development, what about the APC-ness of it all? That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation. We’ve got the APC logo on the dial and the buckle, plus the brand’s guitar-and-dagger insignia engraved out of sight on the caseback. Casio already offers the regular A1000 in a bunch of different colorways, but these two latest ones are made specifically for the APC collab. The release includes a silver case with a dark-green dial and another in gold on gold. Both of the pieces have a brushed sun-ray effect on the dial. The vibe is refined and stripped back; this is a fashion watch that almost feels anti-fashion.

Maybe the best way to think about it is as the reverse side of the coin to the excellent new G-Shock 2500 Series. Both come from Casio, and both are minimal and functional. But the G-Shocks are major and bulky, with a design that seems to tip its hat to Patek Philippe’s Nautilus. These new ones are slim and nearly dressy. Put the two new releases together, and you’ve got pretty much all bases covered. And if those aforementioned Timex collabs felt a bit too classicist for you, then the Casio-APC partnership takes things in a more modern direction. Far from just being a cash grab, the “fashion watch” is now one of the best routes into affordable, on-point horology.

In a recent development, opening a boutique is a delicate exercise in materials and mood to bring its world to life in a physical space. So it makes sense that for Karin Soderlind, Kristina Tjader, and Sofia Wallenstam, the sisters and founders behind Stockholm-based Dagmar, their Alyssa Kapito-designed flagship became a strong point of reference. When Wallenstam, the brand’s creative director, went looking for inspiration for pre-spring ‘27, the debut collection from new design director Rachael Proud, formerly creative director of Raey, the two didn’t need to look further than the walls of its new shop.

“When Rachel and I started to look at what the collection should be, we looked at our store,” Wallenstam shares with Vogue. In the flagship, a metal Jean Prouvé piece hangs on the wall alongside a handcrafted André Sornay sofa, and the tension between the two became the collection’s throughline. “The Prouvé piece on the wall is metal, quite hard, almost brutalist, and then we have this beautiful soft boucle sofa,” she says. “That was the meeting point, the hard versus the soft.”.

It has been revealed that launching November 19 alongside a newly introduced brand identity, the 130-piece pre-spring collection spans relaxed denim (a favorite of Wallenstam’s), sharp-shouldered tailoring, a croc pencil skirt, open-cut tanks, suede outerwear, and boots, much of it drawing on the textures and tones of the store. “We wanted to reuse the bouclé, not in the same way obviously, but that feeling of it,” Wallenstam says. The colors, too—the blacks, whites, and browns—feel representative of the Dagmar woman, Wallenstam adds.

Industry observers note that the collection also marks a upcoming chapter for the Dagmar woman, who Wallenstam describes as confident and living a busy, bustling life with a packed calendar. “She might go and have a school drop-off and go straight to a meeting, and then meet friends, go to a dinner,” she shares. “She wants to look smart and she wants to look cool at the same time.” With Proud on board, that approach is getting a little more edge, with roomier silhouettes and sharper shoulders at the forefront. It’s a bit more oversized than Dagmar has done in the past, with warmer tones integrated throughout. Wallenstam also pushes back on the notion of minimalism, so often pinned on Scandinavian fashion. “Of course, we have neutral tones, but it has heritage. It has a depth to it and a warmth to it.”.

Recent findings suggest that as for how she and Proud approached the collection together, “When Rachel and I first sat down to discuss what the collection should be and how it should feel, we started immediately with the Dagmar woman and what’s vital to her,” Wallenstam indicates. And the pencil skirt is where Proud’s influence really shows. “You can really see the meeting point between Rachel and Dagmar in the pencil skirt,” she says. “It’s a very feminine product, but it has an elastic waist to make it more relaxed, and it’s in croco, which is a little bit harder in the material.” It’s the piece in the collection that will feel as comfortable at your desk as it does at dinner—a full expression of the latest Dagmar approach. It’s the Prouvé and the bouclé sofa all over again, translated into a single skirt. And of course, the same push and pull runs through the rest of the collection.

Prices range from $140 to $3,300, and Vogue readers can exclusively shop the collection on Dagmar for 24 hours, before its official launch on November 20; retailer drops on Net-a-Porter and Nordstrom to follow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart. Music booms over the speakers and other competitors shuffle around the cavernous room of the Armory Track in Washington Heights, Latest York, but Krepack stays laser-focused, thanks to years of meditation practice.

According to recent reports, as soon as the volunteer claims “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over. As he lands on the other side, he sprints to the beam, dropping down into an army crawl. “Take your time, take your time,” his son yells from the sidelines. Krepack reaches the far end, rushes back, and repeats the sequence again before crossing the line in 51 seconds. To cool down, he paces back and forth with his hands on his head. “I think I’m a sprinter, I’m a jumper, but then it’s like, fuck, no, I’m 73 years old,” he says, catching his breath.

The challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging. On November 7th, the inaugural day-long event drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries, and about 70% of participants were between the ages of 40 and 64. Krepeck agreed to let me shadow him to understand this new event through the lens of someone who is, in fact, aging, and would like to do so gracefully.

Sources indicate that the name of the Games comes from a buzzword that originated in the longevity world: super ager. The term was originally coined by Northwestern University researchers to describe adults over 80 whose memories rival those of people 30 years younger. These days it’s thrown around on podcasts and in books to describe anyone who defies both the typical trajectory of both cognitive and physical aging.

The inaugural Super Age Games drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries.

Industry observers note that from crawling across a cargo net to reading microexpressions, the challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill. At the end, athletes see where they rank among their age group and receive their “Super Age,” learning how their body’s physical fitness stacks up against the general U.S. population’s.

In an era where your average middle-aged midwestern dad is training for Hyrox, and a latest, outlandishly extreme challenge is being invented every few months, the Super Age games are a low-key counterpoint to raw, stunty, athleticism, born from the metric-obsessed fitness subcultures who prize longevity above all. And now that fitness trackers like Whoop or Apple Watch can track VO2max, heart rate variability, and resting heart rates, that group continues to grow. Along the way, these stats have become status symbols on par with owning a Lamborghini. And now that overall health is quantifiable, fitness values have become less about just how fast you run or how much you lift, but how slowly aging.

Recent findings suggest that it follows that, despite its name, Super Age Games isn’t just for aging athletes. The crowd there leaned middle-aged, and the youngest person at the competition was 21. As we stood by the dead hang station, Krepak pointed across the room at a brolic young man who looked like he could be an NFL prospect: “That dude’s a serious athlete,” he says, as we watched him run around the track cradling a sandbag on his shoulder.

Unlike competitions like Hyrox, where athletes race through a sequence of workouts against the clock, the Super Age Games allows competitors to rest as long as they need between trials. In fact, Junior Kennedy, the fitness program director for the Games, encourages it. “There's no rush,” he says. “The goal is to get through each event as intentionally as you can. We need to understand what it means to recover.”.

Each trial was developed with a certain longevity marker in mind, and developed with input from researchers at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, a leading nonprofit research center based in Novato, California dedicated to understanding aging. The Over Under, for example, tests agility by judging how fast you can change levels and switch directions. Meanwhile, the Synapse, a challenge where participants track moving balls on a screen and identify them after they've been shuffled around, is meant to measure cognitive processing.

Challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill.

Krepack, a psychologist and lifelong athlete from Mill Valley, California, first heard about the event through its founder, David Stewart. Stewart is a media founder behind two niche longevity platforms, AGEIST and Super Age, where he writes about longevity, wellness, and redefining aging (one of his website testimonial’s states he has made aging “cool and aspirational.”). Krepack’s generally a skeptic of the profit-driven modern wellness industry—“I've always had a jaded view of all of that stuff,” he says—but he has followed both Stewart and the Buck Institutes’ work for years.

Industry observers note that the competition appealed to Krepack, in part because he’s spent decades cultivating a consistent exercise routine he’s proud of. He played baseball in college and has spent much of his life skiing, cycling, and playing other sports. These days, his schedule revolves around a handful of rituals: bike rides on Mondays and Fridays, a Saturday hike with a friend, gardening, yoga, and Zen meditation most days. When he signed up for the Games in June, he altered his exercise routine, lifted more weights, practiced hanging from a bar, and experimented with the Neurotracker cognitive test online.

According to recent reports, yet all that training didn’t prepare Krepack for the biggest surprise of his day. After scoring well on both the Inferno (the assault bike VO2max test) and Synapse, next came the fourth trial: the “Tightrope,” a balance challenge that requires competitors to walk along a low beam while carrying a water-filled bag, taking as many consecutive steps as they can in two minutes without falling. He had expected to excel, thanks to years of skiing and yoga. Instead, he struggled to keep steady as the water shifted inside the bag. As his foot slipped off the bar, his eyes got wide. “I can’t believe my balance,” he notes. “That’s my one disappointment in life now.”.

Alan Krepack's sons Harrison and Aaron during the “tightrope” challenge.

Krepack was still hard on himself as we walked over to the dead hang trial. But after beating both his sons’ times, he seemed to get his competitive spirit back. He pushed through the remaining challenge determined to finish strong. And he did: By the end of the Games, he had placed second overall, with scores adjusted for age.

Industry observers note that A few days after the competition, I checked in with Krepack to ask him how he’d processed the event. He responded with screenshots of his scores. His highest score came from the cargo net, which he credited to sheer determination rather than any particular finesse: “due to my will and overcoming an unconventional and desperate style!” he texted me, “Plus my sons were great support and focus partners.”.

According to recent reports, but the Games were also a reality check about aging: “I left there feeling both young and old,” he tells me on a phone call. As he watched his sons rocket through the obstacles, he was forced to confront how much of his athleticism he’d lost. “They just flew over it. They were so fluid, and so fast,” he says. “I’m not 30 or 40 or 50 or 60 anymore.”.

Despite all the longevity industry's promises of maintaining youth, Krepack sees little value in denying the inevitable. Aging well, he indicates, is about “accepting, improving, and doing your best. It’s not a denial of who you are at this point in life.” The goal, he says, is to make the most of what you’re still capable of.

What Are Thanksgiving Sides That Don't Need to Go in the Oven?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here.

On Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey. In years past, the stress of getting everything in and out of the oven with the right amount of time has been a nuisance that I’d like to avoid this year. Are there any Thanksgiving sides that feel classic but don’t need the oven? —Oven-whelmed.

Recent findings suggest that if there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bull’s-eye. (And as someone who has never hit a real bull’s-eye in her life, I mean this as quite the compliment!) Even if you place oven racks strategically—even if you have one of those fancy double ovens—there’s always a bottleneck of dishes that need to be roasted and baked.

The solution is not to plot out an overwrought schedule of when things go in and out, and in and out, but to ruthlessly reduce the number of recipes that require the oven in the first place.

Industry observers note that with that in mind, I would like to point out that turkey can thrive in other settings. And no, I’m not talking about deep-frying it in your yard, which we all know is a rowdy and risky idea, as proven in Gilmore Girls season three, episode nine. You could grill it. You could smoke it. Both delightful.

It has been revealed that but you asked about sides specifically, so sides are what we will tackle today. Beyond the classics like mashed potatoes, boxed stuffing, and cranberry sauce, here are 10 recipes that do not need an oven at all—and brazenly, boldly get away with it.

Industry observers note that green Beans and Mushrooms With Crispy Shallots. The same cozy flavors as a classic green bean casserole—earthy mushrooms, frizzled shallots—but it comes together entirely on the stovetop. Now is the time to branch beyond white button or baby bella; opt for shiitake or oyster, the wonkier the shape the better.

Industry observers note that green Beans With Tahini Sbagliato. For something less traditional, from Samin Nosrat’s recent cookbook, this recipe is make-ahead-friendly on multiple fronts. You can blanch the green beans a day ahead and whip up the tahini-miso sauce up to four days ahead. All that’s left on Turkey Day is assembly.

Brussels Sprouts Stir-Fry With Cheddar and Golden Raisins. Thinly sliced and swiftly sautéed, brussels sprouts take on a savory char. The cheddar could be swapped out for Gouda, or any aged cheese you love. Likewise, the golden raisins could be replaced with dried cranberries or chopped dates. It’s flexible!

It has been revealed that air Fryer Crispy Brussels Sprouts With Honey Butter. Or free up the stove and turn to your trusty air fryer instead. In the concentrated and circulating heat, the sprouts’ outer leaves become crackly like potato chips, craveable enough to go back for thirds.

Sweet Potatoes With Tahini Butter. Most sweet potatoes in our archive are roasted, so isn’t it ironic that one of our most popular recipes is steamed. Author Carla Lalli puts it perfectly: “Steaming offers extreme speed and high hydration, which means that whatever you cook will be done swiftly and always moist. Sweet potatoes in particular benefit from this treatment, which makes their flesh pudding-like and fluffy.”.

Glazed Carrots. Li’l retro! These saucy carrots are sweet but not too sweet thanks to a floral mixture of orange juice and honey, plus a welcome zing from fresh ginger. I could see parsnips swapping in happily here.

In a recent development, parsnip Purée. Speaking of parsnips, from the Barefoot Contessa herself, this is a cousin to mashed potatoes that, in my humble opinion, is a whole lot better. Parsnips have a je ne sais quois, needing no more than butter, salt, and pepper, to shine bright.

It has been revealed that adult Mac and Cheese. Despite its title, this dish will be a hit with grown-ups and kids alike. It comes together on the stove with just six ingredients (and that’s including salt!). A few of its rave reviews: “Staple now in my house,” “Super easy and always delicious!” and “Lovelovelove. I’ve made this so many times.” Medium shells catch the sauce like little canoes; or could be a fun moment for radiatori.

Kale Salad With Pecan Vinaigrette. Pecans are good for more than pie. Here they turn into a nutty dressing for ruffled kale and perky radishes. Though salad is not the first (or even second) thing one might think of for Thanksgiving, it has become an absolute must on my family’s table. A refreshing reprieve to all the richness. We have more great options here.

Industry observers note that instant Pot Collard Greens. On a holiday table, when there’s so much going on, sometimes a simple dish is just the thing. Bacon, greens, onion, chile, done. An Instant Pot is like a Thanksgiving cheat code, freeing up the oven and the stove too.

Readers, what sides are you making this year for Thanksgiving? Share menu inspiration in the comments!

Questions may be lightly edited for clarity, length, and style.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so blueprint ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

Sources indicate that whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Industry observers note that turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

According to recent reports, place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

In a recent development, unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Industry observers note that place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Willy Chavarria and Raul Lopez of Luar are among the designers participating in “Malvestir,” a major fresh exhibition at MoMA PS1 that examines the relationship between Latin American fashion and contemporary art. Unveiled today and opening April 22, 2027, the exhibition will feature work by 20 artists and designers from across the Americas, bringing together clothing, photography, sculpture, and textiles to explore how dress reflects questions of cultural identity, class, and power.

In a recent development, for Chavarria and Lopez, whose respective designs draw on their Chicano and Dominican American backgrounds, these conversations have long been part of their work. Both have built internationally recognized labels that incorporate the aesthetics and experiences of communities historically underrepresented within luxury fashion.

It has been revealed that “Being part of this exhibition at MoMA PS1 is deeply meaningful to me,” Chavarria tells Vogue. “It’s an opportunity to share a piece of who I am, where I come from, and the culture that has shaped me. I’m proud to be part of a moment that gives space to Latino voices and celebrates the beauty, creativity, and richness of our culture.”.

It has been revealed that josh Tafoya. Bad Hombre. 2026. Hand-woven Serape-style cape in Churro wool. Multi panels with Rio Grande, Chimayo, and Vallero styles. Hand-sewn with natural-dyed wool warp. With spotted black and white hair on hide chaps. Hand-cut fringe. Courtesy of the artist.

According to recent reports, lopez, meanwhile, has built Luar around his experiences growing up in New York, drawing on Dominican culture, queer nightlife, and the city’s ever-shifting approach to getting dressed. “I grew up in New York in a Dominican family, around people who could make a whole look out of whatever they had,” Lopez tells Vogue. “The fashion industry has always pulled from communities like mine. With Luar, I’ve always wanted us to be the ones telling those stories. Being part of “Malvestir” at MoMA PS1 feels personal because I get to bring that point of view into the room alongside artists and designers with their own stories about what it means to get dressed across Latin America and the diaspora.”.

It has been revealed that the exhibition’s title offers some insight into its broader themes. Combining the Spanish words mal (“poorly”) and vestir (“to dress”), “Malvestir” references the colonial-era designation malvestidos, applied to those whose clothing did not conform to prescribed boundaries of race, caste, or gender. The term remains pejorative but can also express a rejection of established conventions of taste and social class. The exhibition considers these histories alongside the ways artists and designers use clothing to express identity today.

Leonardo Choxom. Performance, from the series Piezas Experimentales, 2023–2024. Textile. Courtesy of the artist. © Leonardo Choxom.

José Ballivian. La virgen viste de Balenciaga. 2024. Pencil on paper. 100 x 70 cm. Courtesy of the artist.

Recent findings suggest that organized by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, “Malvestir” will bring together artists working across a wide range of disciplines. Colombian photographer Camila Falquez’s ongoing series Syncretism, for example, features portraits of queer and trans people from Latin America and the Caribbean, drawing on Indigenous and African spiritual traditions. Mexican designer Carla Fernández, known for her collaborations with Indigenous artisans, will also participate, alongside Bolivian artist José Ballivián, whose drawings place familiar luxury and sportswear logos within traditional Andean imagery.

Other works address the global movement of clothing and its environmental and economic consequences. Guatemalan artist David Ramírez Cotón draws on his family’s experience running a secondhand clothing business in Guatemala City, while Venezuelan artist Cassandra Mayela uses garments collected from Venezuelan migrants in her large-scale woven works. The Afro-Colombian collective Las Tejedoras de Mampuján will contribute a newly commissioned tapestry depicting the reuse and recycling of textiles within its workshop. The influence of Western luxury and beauty advertising is also examined: Costa Rican artist La Cholla Jackson, for instance, reimagines a Dior campaign from the 2000s, posing with accessories constructed from discarded materials.

Barbara Sánchez-Kane. Lessons in Draping. 2023, rawhide, metal, wood. 325 × 92 × 84 cm. Image courtesy of the artist and Kurimanzutto, Mexico City / Fresh York. © Bárbara Sánchez-Kane. Photo: Da Brandica.

Patrica Belli. Mamá (detail). 2021. Clothing, rope, buckles. 194 x 335 x 172 cm. Courtesy of the artist and Parallel Oaxaca.

“‘Malvestir’ reimagines how fashion can be displayed in museums, reflecting the very alive possibilities and contradictions inherent to the form,” Ketelsen González tells Vogue. “The show offers a provocative, materially rich look at 20 artists and designers across the Americas who are in dialogue with one another yet have never been brought together in an exhibition until now.”.

“Malvestir” arrives amid a wider cultural interest in fashion as a means of exploring identity, heritage, and power. Following the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s 2025 exhibition “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style,” which examined the history of Black dandyism and its relationship to identity across the Atlantic diaspora, the MoMA PS1 show continues a broader conversation about the cultural and political significance of dress. It also builds on MoMA PS1’s own history of presenting fashion alongside contemporary art, dating back to its experimental fashion programming in the early 1980s.

Sources indicate that installation View: Se abrió paca, David Ramírez Cotón. All pieces acrylic on canvas, variable measurements, 2024. Curated by Josseline Pinto at La Galería Rebelde, Guatemala City. Photo: courtesy of La Galería Rebelde.

Willy Chavarria. Safe from Harm (still), 2024. Courtesy of the artist and MATTE. © Willy Chavarria.

“‘Malvestir’ addresses urgent, shared concerns across fashion, contemporary art, and visual culture, engaging daring artists and designers both in New York and across the Americas,” Butler notes. “MoMA PS1 has a history of presenting innovative designers alongside contemporary artists. We’re thrilled that audiences will be able to experience the formal experimentation, political imagination, and cultural contradictions at the heart of ‘Malvestir.’”.

“Malvestir” will be on view at MoMA PS1 from April 22 through September 6, 2027.

I’m A Professional Cook & My Secret To Perfectly Smooth Gravy Is This $4 Pantry Staple

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gravy is one of the most problematic dishes on the Thanksgiving table.
  • Sources indicate that making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic.
  • In a recent development, the secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gravy is one of the most problematic dishes on the Thanksgiving table. Every year, home cooks struggle and sweat over gravy that’s too thin, too greasy, or—worst of all—lumpy. All while your relatives watch and the turkey gets cold.

Sources indicate that making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic. But on holidays when prepping ahead just isn’t in the cards, one simple hack can solve your gravy woes: a $4 pantry staple that will thicken up any gravy in mere minutes—without any lumps.

In a recent development, the secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour. Known to chefs and home cooks alike for its bright blue cylindrical can, Wondra is wheat flour that has been pre-gelatinized, dried, and finely milled so it dissolves more easily and thickens sauces faster than regular flour. This means you can whisk it directly into any gravy (no matter the temperature!) without worry about clumping—and it will thicken that gravy almost immediately.

According to recent reports, if you’re making gravy from scratch with no other thickener besides Wondra, I recommend starting with 1 tablespoon for every cup of stock and/or drippings. You can do this by heating the drippings or stock in a pot on the stove, then just whisking in the Wondra. It should thicken within a few minutes. If your drippings don’t have a ton of fat, I recommend whisking in a little butter too, to help with the flavor.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re using Wondra to troubleshoot a gravy that’s too thin, I recommend whisking in a few teaspoons at a time. The Wondra should do its thickening magic within a minute or two after it goes in, and then you can decide whether you need more.

Sources indicate that while Wondra flour is great for thickening gravies and sauces, it’s far from a one-trick pony. I’ve used it to coat white fish (such as tilapia) before pan-searing to give it a beautifully thin, crispy crust—and help prevent the fish from sticking to the pan. It’s also a common ingredient in batters for fried foods, since its lower protein content helps form a lighter, crispier crust—and it’s also a magical way to get a flakier pastry dough. So even if you only make gravy once a year, that blue canister won’t go to waste.

In a recent development, it’s possible that Rufus Sewell is having too much fun right now. Between playing morally ambiguous Vice President (and husband to the U.S. Ambassador to the Court of St. James’s) Hal Wyler in Netflix’s frothy, prestige-y series The Diplomat and the beloved but deeply flawed Mr. Bennet in the streamer’s upcoming adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, he’s cornered the market on lovable rascals. He thrives on “exercises in gray” and relishes “when it goes wrong” for a character. “It’s the opposite of what you want in life,” he tells me. “You want drama, you want mistakes.” These roles offer plenty of both.

Wyler, of The Diplomat, is navigating how to work with the increasingly autocratic and bloody-minded President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) thousands of miles away from his wife Kate (Keri Russell), who is starting to exhibit some of his own manipulative behaviors she claims to abhor. Two centuries prior, Mr. Bennet is reckoning not with geopolitical crises and egomaniacal heads of state, but with the challenges his wife faces in marrying off five eligible, if dowry-poor, daughters.

Sewell sat down for a long chat with GQ about the two series, the value of blending high silliness with high stakes in the same scene, and how bodily functions are an under-appreciated key to unlocking a character’s specificity.

Industry observers note that rufus Sewell: The interesting question for me, for the second half of the season, was how much is Hal truly aware of everything that Kate and everyone else are noticing and concerned about with Grace's behavior. How much does he see? How much is he choosing to pretend not to see in order to stay in the room? He's always believed that access is all, but how much do you compromise in order to stay in the room? Where’s the point when you realize you stayed in the room too long without saying anything, and the moment’s passed, and you are just an accomplice? I found it very difficult to play his seeming unctuousness and obsequiousness with Grace this season, and to not be trying to protect my character in the wrong way, because I felt he was failing.

According to recent reports, he’s overestimated his ability to effect change with Grace. Hal was prepared to appear to be supporting her, when he believed in his ability to steer her in a better direction, and I think he goes past that point. When I read the final episode script and saw where he ends up walking out, it gave me the courage to really lean into how much he goes wrong, by his own standards earlier in the season. He begins to lose his way in a way that he never has done before. But I embraced it, knowing that the real gift of the part was getting to play him going wrong and then seemingly correcting himself. We actually shot a speech that he made, just to give us a sense of where the scene was headed and for me to know how to play it. They might end up using some of it in the next season, or they could end up completely changing what was written. Hal coming out of the summit is a momentous decision in terms of what that does for the future and I've got no idea what’s next—I can't wait to start filming season five to find out.

In a recent development, I was always shocked when this show was described as a thriller because I always thought it was a kind of romantic sex comedy with extremely high stakes, because what it reminded me of firstly was some of the comedy of divorce screwball films of the 1940s. The characters may be divorced after a very tempestuous relationship, but they’re interlinked in a way that can never be undone. There's a romance to all of that history.

According to recent reports, the other thing that it reminded me of was the kind of films that were made in the '70s—French films where halfway through an argument one of the characters would sit down on the toilet, you know what I mean? The people inside these films remind you of your own relationships. Your long-term relationship might not go to the same extremes, it might not be in the same setting, but I think people are people. What I love about their relationship is their shared wonkiness, and the getting into the nitty-gritty of the politics and taking someone down and hatching a plot whilst fighting over pastries and getting crumbs on the bed—all of that is part of their foreplay.

Industry observers note that that is what the show is about, as far as I'm concerned. These are people who wear suits that might stand at a lectern and be on TV, but the fact is, how do you scratch an itch? Do you smell? Do you need to go to the toilet? These are the things that the script leans into a lot, and it might put some people off, but I don't care about that. That's the thing that makes it feel real, and it's so refreshing to play.

It has been revealed that he'll flirt with anyone. We all know people like this. It's not even necessarily sexual, he just engages with people on that level and it's a natural thing for him.

I would say Hal’s flirtatiousness being a problem is open for debate, because a lot of what we understand of him is via Kate’s descriptions of him and his behavior. I can and often do see it in a different way. Part of the story of seasons three and four is Kate’s realization that a lot of stuff she thought of as his personality was in fact the mantle of the job that he'd taken on, because we see her doing the same kinds of things now that she is an ambassador. They both have a lot of the same qualities. They're both killers in a sense, and it's been very convenient for her and great for the show for her to introduce the public to Hal through her descriptions. And yet, every time it seems like he's changed character, in fact, it is revealing something from a different perspective.

Recent findings suggest that we learned pretty early on that we were going to be doing some very, very long scenes, and we were given the advantage of seeing the scenes very early so we could slowly gestate the performances. We needed that because Windsor Castle in the show was comprised of several different buildings and locations, some of them with oceans between them, so we’d be shooting some parts the next day, and other bits in four months’ time.

Recent findings suggest that especially with a two-hander, with such long takes, you can go in and out of being relaxed, unrelaxed, free, slightly bound, and actually you get to the point where you stop worrying about it. It's like being on stage, because you end up too tired to be bad all the time and end up inhabiting the moment and things just happen. I love that all of it was a surprise to us.

I think what is most vital in this particular iteration of the relationship between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet is that he comes to realize which ways he's failed his daughters. When Mrs. Bennet states to him in this version, it's easy for you to say that I’m silly or frivolous, but you try being a woman at this age with no means—this is the fight of their lives that he is making these jokes about. And yes, of course he's funny and right in certain ways, but he's also guilty of negligence of his family for the sake of an easy life for himself. The reason they have no money is that so much money has been spent on bonnets. Money could have been saved, but in order to have a quiet life, he's ducked out of fights in order to avoid responsibility.

Exactly. It was a gift in this role to have that moment when he feels that, admits that, and gets to be slightly humbled in this idea of himself that he's been cultivating. He didn’t actively or consciously avoid having this revelation, but that’s the effect of staying in his study, and now he’s facing the consequences. To use very modern terms, he has a revelation of what his pattern has been. It made sense!

Industry observers note that one could be forgiven for thinking that Mr. and Mrs. Bennet are two people that used to be attracted to each other and now have nothing in common and don't like each other. I think it's born out in the book, though, the idea that there is still a love there, and especially a shared humor between them, and a bit of a spark remains.

I love the fact that we get to get drunk together and stuff like that. Olivia Colman and I worked on The Father together a few years ago with Anthony Hopkins, which was a very different kind of gig, but as is often the case with things that are very heavy and intense, we had a hoot doing it. I loved working with her, and was very excited about the chance to work with her again. I love the scenes between Mr. Bennet and Mrs. Bennet. They were such a treat for us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Industry observers note that spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

It has been revealed that bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

Sources indicate that ever since Starbucks started co-opting seemingly every street corner and strip mall and multiple waves of coffee snobbery (laudatory) have risen in direct opposition to mass market espresso, it’s safe to say the average consumer has changed what they expect from a cup of coffee. Just look at the coffee maker aisle in any massive-box store and, along with single-serve and pod machines and other barista-replacing gadgets, you’ll find a slew of coffee makers that promise to make you dozens of drink styles, froth up some milk, and bring you “instant” cold brew. But sometimes the simplest way to make coffee is still pretty darn good. What we’re saying is don’t discount the drip coffee machine.

In a recent development, the cliché of bad drip coffee from a cheap piece of plastic doesn’t apply anymore. And even lots of cheap coffee makers are so much better than they used to be. If you’re in the market for a lot of coffee with little effort, your options are now legion. Companies like Breville, Fellow, Oxo, and Ratio have joined the original king of drip, Technivorm, in making quality appliances that better control factors like water temperature, flow rate, and bloom time, several of which brew coffee that’s almost as good as what you can get with a kettle and a pour-over setup.

Our writers and editors have tested more than three dozen coffee makers over the years, and below we get into the ones that make a good cup of coffee, the ones that make a great cup of coffee, and the unfortunate ones that just can’t keep up with today’s coffee-brewing arms race.

New in this revision: We tested two new coffee makers with plastic-free brewing systems from Caraway and Simply Good Coffee. We also tested the new Braun OptiBrew Pro, which includes an onboard milk frother among other features.

Capacity: 10 cupsCarafe style: ThermalDimensions: 8.9" x 8.9" x 12"Weight: 9.6 lb.Features: Adjustable brew water ratio; adjustable temperature settings, flavor profile settings, programmable 24-hour timer; Wi-Fi connectivity; cold-brew capable; SCA Golden Cup capabilitiesWarranty: 3 years.
