Sources indicate that the secondhand market is chock full of navy-blue hoodies that have been sun-faded and beaten down with time. They'll cost you just as much as this Mfpen version, but will also fall apart faster than you can zip 'em up.

In a recent development, les Tien's dedication to all things sweats results in a catalog of luxurious fleece and terry cloth with a modern approach. Featuring high-end Cobrax hardware, RiRi zippers, raw-edge hems and sleeves, and a heavyweight brushed fleece, no detail is phoned in.

The Real McCoy's is considered by many to be Americana repro wizards. This revival of an early 20th-Century hoodie is just one small piece of the brand's preservation prowess. It's made using beefy sinker-knit fleece, old-school Talon-style zippers, and vertical patch pockets.

Sources indicate that A.Presse's chokehold on the menswear illuminati refuses to let up and it's pieces like this vintage-inspired hoodie that keep the pressure on. Based on very rare “after-hood parkas", this made-in-Japan hoodie features an idiosyncratic attached hood, super dense and lofty fleece, with artfully distressed details throughout.

Think of the zip-up as the pullover hoodie's elder brother, but with way more layering potential. In its most natural state, it can cuddle up to a matching set of sweatpants and a baggy tee with flair. (Top it off with a swanky necklace, crisp sneakers, and some stellar shades and you’re left with a fit on par with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at his tunnel-trotting best.).

Sources indicate that unzipped and left open, it can also take on the role of a picture frame ready to display your sickest graphic tee—much like the cardigan, another treasure of 2000s fashion. Or make like a mid-Aughts garage band ironically donning corporate attire and wear your zip-up over a dress shirt and baggy tailored trousers, a high-minded fashion move with a jolt of kooky Scandinavian cool.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

It has been revealed that our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

According to recent reports, to kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

It has been revealed that we lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Sources indicate that across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally upcoming to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

#54410. Tech Report: Why You Should Never Put Frozen Meat In A Slow Cooker, According To Experts

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (770 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Delish ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why You Should Never Put Frozen Meat In A Slow Cooker, According To Experts

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that with busy schedules and limited time each day, slow cookers are key to getting dinner on the table.
  • Recent findings suggest that but think again.
  • Sorry to be the bearer of bad news: You should never put frozen meat directly into your slow cooker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with busy schedules and limited time each day, slow cookers are key to getting dinner on the table. They can take simple ingredients and transform them into a complete, ready-to-eat meal. Because the slow cooker does all the work for you, you may think that it can also handle defrosting meat.

Recent findings suggest that but think again. The idea seems convenient in theory, but in practice, it raises some serious food safety concerns. We consulted health experts to learn more about adding frozen meat to a slow cooker. So next time you proposal a hands-off dinner, you can make sure your food is delicious and safe to eat.

Sorry to be the bearer of bad news: You should never put frozen meat directly into your slow cooker. “I am all for cutting out unnecessary steps in cooking, but using frozen meat in your slow cooker is not one of them,” claims Melissa Koch, RD, MEd.

Raw meat can carry harmful bacteria that cause foodborne illness. Freezing stops them from multiplying, but doesn't necessarily kill them. And because slow cookers heat food gradually, frozen meat can spend too long in what food safety experts call the “temperature danger zone.”.

Sources indicate that “The danger zone refers to a temperature range of 40°F (4°C) to 140°F (60°C) over two or more hours when harmful bacteria grow or multiply at a fast rate,” Koch explains. It can take hours for food in a slow cooker to move above the danger zone—and starting with frozen meat delays that process even further.

“The appliance heats food slowly, and starting with frozen meat means the internal temperature may sit in the ‘danger zone’ for too long,” says chef and dietitian Sharniquia White. “This gives bacteria like Salmonella or E. coli more opportunity to multiply before the food reaches a safe cooking temperature.”.

Sources indicate that what happens after eating food that has sat in the danger zone? The consequences vary based on your immune system, the extent of the contamination, and the strains of bacteria present. But none are pleasant, and some may even send you to the hospital.

“Symptoms of food-borne illness can include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and fever,” Koch indicates. “You can experience the effects of food-borne illness within a few minutes to days after consuming a load of harmful pathogens or bacteria.”.

In a recent development, cooking frozen meat on the “low” setting of your slow cooker increases the time it spends in the danger zone, but the risk is present regardless. “The 'high' setting reduces the amount of time food spends at unsafe temperatures, but still doesn’t fully eliminate the risk when starting with frozen meat,” states White.

Industry observers note that the ingredients you're using can also increase your risk. “Larger, denser cuts (like roasts or whole poultry) take longer to thaw and heat evenly, so they pose a greater risk of staying at unsafe temperatures for extended periods,” White explains.

Smaller pieces may thaw faster, but that doesn't necessarily make them safe to cook from frozen. White explains that ground meat is “particularly risky” because of the way it's processed, so it should be cooked thoroughly.

“I feed three young children at my home, so in my opinion, I wouldn't chance cooking frozen meat, no matter the size, in a slow cooker,” Koch says.

The answer is simple: thaw your meat before turning on your slow cooker. But your ideal method depends on how much time you have.

In a recent development, the safest, easiest, and least involved thawing method is to put your frozen meat in the fridge. The cold temperature of your refrigerator lets your food defrost gently without entering the danger zone.

Our editors recommend placing the meat on a plate or baking sheet to collect any juices and avoid contaminating other food in your fridge. This process can take anywhere from a couple of hours to a couple of days, depending on the cut of meat. “This requires some thought and effort, but in the long run it's worth your safety,” Koch notes.

No time for that? No problem. You can thaw meat faster by submerging it in cold water in a leakproof bag, changing the water every 30 minutes, or defrosting it in the microwave, though the latter can compromise the meat's texture. Both methods require cooking the meat immediately afterward. “Once thawed, meat should go directly into the slow cooker,” White explains.

It all takes a little extra effort and planning, but it's worth it to avoid getting sick from your slow cooker dinner.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop. But the best cutting boards do more than just protect your counters during food prep—they provide a stable surface when you’re vigorously chopping and act as a protective surface that prevents prematurely dulling the blades of your kitchen knives. Cutting boards come in a variety of materials: plastic, wood, rubber, even glass and metal for inexplicable reasons. After testing dozens of boards of all sorts of materials over the course of six years, we have found five favorites. Read on to find out which might be best for you as well as how we tested and what we look for in the cutting boards we want to use every day.

New in this upgrade: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options. They’re easier on knives and more beautiful to keep on the counter. And our new top pick is reasonably priced as end-grain boards go. For more on what makes end- and edge-grain boards different, click here. And if you’re looking for a quality (but truly inexpensive) wood board, we’d encourage you to look at these two Boos boards. They’re edge-grain, so they’ll wear your knives more promptly, but Boos makes almost universally great cutting boards.

Maple End-Grain Cutting Board (18" x 12").

In a recent development, A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment. A good wood cutting board can last decades and decades, and since it will likely live permanently on your counter, function as a key aesthetic component of your kitchen. Our editors have used this heavy-duty piece for over a year in their home kitchens, and even after daily use, it shows little to no wear and only minimal staining.

In a recent development, what we love: The craftsmanship on the board is apparent as soon as you take it out of the box. The offset pattern of the individual pieces of wood is striking (as it is on most end-grain boards). And its construction feels smooth and solid.

It has been revealed that as an end-grain board, it’s easy on knife blades, leaving them sharper than a less expensive edge-grain board. The real highlights, beyond the pure aesthetics, are in the small design features, though. Senior shopping editor Noah Kaufman has been using it in his home kitchen since June of 2025 and has found it the most stable board he’s ever used. That’s thanks to the addition of four grippy silicone-tipped feet on one side (you can order a Boardsmith without the feet, but you’d be giving away that stability). Those feet also raise the board up a little higher on the counter—which prevents the underside from retaining moisture and warping—and for Noah, they elevate the board to a very comfortable cutting height. It’s also reversible, with an effective, though not too deep, juice groove on the side of the footed side.

Recent findings suggest that boardsmith’s end-grain boards are very customizable. They come in four sizes (we tested the 18" x 12" x 2", but the largest—24" x 18" x 2"—would make a beautiful always-out piece), three wood types (in addition to the maple, we tried walnut and cherry), and you can opt for features like juice and finger grooves. The feet are also optional, though they’re included by default, so you have to check a box if you want a board without feet.

Recent findings suggest that what we’d leave: Again, this board is heavy, which makes it sturdy, but also a bit of a chore to clean. Because it’s wood, it also requires some upkeep in the form of oiling and buttering (the brand’s Board Butter has kept the surface of the Noah’s board in tip-top shape through months of use). Finally, while the feet are a vital feature, they do make the board a little less attractive if left on the counter with the juice groove facing up. But using the groove is a less frequent use than regular slicing and chopping, so you’ll be more likely to leave it feet side down—or at least turn it back over after you’re done cutting and cleaning.

It has been revealed that in the long run: With long-term testing of a full year, the Boardsmith has stood up in a way that justifies its high price. It’s held on to minimal stains, and with a bit of oil and wax every three to four weeks, the board looks as beautiful as it did when it arrived.

R-Board Series Rectangular Wooden Maple Cutting Board, 18”x12”.

Boos boards, as they’re commonly called, are pretty much the gold standard for wood cutting boards, and this relatively affordable maple cutting board is a dream to cut on.

What we love: Though maple is a hard wood, the cutting surface is smooth and has the perfect amount of give. In our testing, it seemed to almost embrace the knife blade with each chop. The board didn’t retain any food odors and it was easy to hand-wash (never put a wood board in the dishwasher!). Even beet juice disappeared after a good cleaning.

Industry observers note that boos Blocks come in many different sizes, we’ve found that the 18x12" size is just right for most home kitchens. This board is from the brand’s R-Board series, and it’s substantial without being too big. There’s plenty of room to carve a roast chicken, but it’s small enough to slide into the cabinet where you keep your sheet pans (a half-sheet is 18x13") as long as you don’t have too much else in there. At 2.25" it’s the tallest (thickest) cutting board we tested, and it will add significant height to your cooking zone, which is something shorter home cooks should always keep in mind when choosing a chopping board.

What we’d leave: Though not necessarily a negative, this board is on the heavy side (10 lb.), and it does require frequent oiling to keep it in tip-top shape. Boos recommends their proprietary Mystery Oil and Board Cream, and if you buy directly from the brand, you can bundle the care products with the board.

What we love: Sonder’s board is beautiful, and like the Boardsmith, it features end-grain construction, which is easier on knives because they slide between the wood fibers, avoiding friction with the hard surface. End-grain boards also “self-heal,” which means that the fibers come back together after having been sliced—and I found that after rigorous use in a week of endless chopping tests, this board came out looking as beautiful as it had when it came out of the package. This board is made of American walnut and constructed in the US.

Recent findings suggest that the Sonder board also has some clever design elements: It’s hard to find an end-grain board that features a juice groove at this price point (the Boardsmith below, for example, costs almost $100 more). Flip the board over, and on the other side, it features three carved-out compartments, so you can slide chopped food to the side as you prep, keeping ingredients contained, separated, and out of the way. Those compartments can also be used for a fun charcuterie board setup: Use them to hold sauces and condiments or as a landing place for olive pits. Both sides of the board feature grippy rubber feet, and I found that this board stayed steady and level on the countertop even during heavy-duty chopping.

In a recent development, this board was less cumbersome to take to the sink and hand wash than many of the large end-grain boards we tried. It has ergonomic handles carved into the sides, which makes for easy transport despite its heft and size. And because it’s a dark-colored wood, it indicates less sign of staining than other wooden boards.

It has been revealed that what we’d leave: There’s not much fault to find in Sonder’s board beyond the standard caveats that an end-grain cutting board requires maintenance in the form of regular oiling and must be hand-washed. The prep grooves are a nice feature, but they aren’t as useful if you’re used to using a bench scraper, since it can’t fit in them. At $179, the Sonder is a bit pricey, but the benefits of end-grain over a cheaper edge-grain board are worth the bump up. If you’re concerned about price primarily, you should opt for the plastic Oxo board recommended below. Because of the carved-in prep containers on one side of the board, you have limited chopping space (but you always have the option to use the other side, which offers a full surface).

What we love: Senior reviews editor, Olivia Tarantino, owns three types of cutting boards (wood, composite, and the MK Midi), and the Midi is the one she grabs for anything short of a full dinner. “It’s closer to midsize than small, which makes it more versatile than a mini board that’s only good for smashing garlic. I can dice a whole onion, slice a tomato, and even fit a mise en place of scallion, ginger, and garlic. Because it’s nonporous, it’s my pick over wood for wetter ingredients, since I can toss it in the dishwasher when I’m done,” she claims, noting that she owns the white color and there’s no staining after eight months. The one downside worth noting is that the surface is a bit harder, which can be tougher on knives.

Adding a smaller board like this to a kitchen that already has a large wood cutting board can help for small prep work like slicing fruit, vegetables, or ingredients like garlic without having to clean your major board in between.

Recent findings suggest that what we’d leave: We wish that Material would add feet to the larger version of the board. If it’s all you’ve got, a small cutting board can be frustratingly limiting. Also, after years of working with Material’s cutting boards in their homes, our editors noted that they will show visible wear and tear in the form of slice marks and small stains. This is inevitable for any plastic (or similar) cutting board.

Good Grips Plastic Utility Cutting Board.

What we love: This plastic cutting board from Oxo is very popular in the BA Test Kitchen. It’s budget-friendly and dishwasher-safe and comes with a juice groove. At 14.75" x 10.4", it’s a good size for meal prep, the plastic cutting surface is nonporous, and silicone strips run the length of both short sides to help keep it in place on the counter when cutting. It’s also reversible with one side offering a channel to catch meat juices.

Sources indicate that what we'd leave: The Oxo isn’t very attractive, so you wouldn’t want to use it as a serving board. Also, the longevity of a plastic board like this is only a couple of years, and if you chop too rigorously, the board has been known to shed plastic particles. If you are concerned about plastic use in the kitchen, this isn’t your board.

Yoshihiro Hi-Soft High Performance Professional Grade Cutting Board.

Rubber cutting boards are seen more often in professional kitchens than home ones, but if you’re looking for something large and durable, and you don’t want to have to bust out your knife sharpener regularly, consider this Hi-Soft rubber board by Yoshihiro. It’s very knife-friendly, and cutting on it feels nice. It stays in place on the counter, and unlike another rubber board we tested, it doesn’t have a rubber tire odor.

What we love: There are a couple of reasons chefs like food-safe rubber cutting surfaces. For starters, because rubber has a little give, the cutting surface flexes ever so slightly to the knife edge versus wearing it down like a hard surface would. Both synthetic and natural rubber are also nonporous, so they’re easier to sanitize than wood boards and are often used by sushi chefs for that reason (conversely, wood cutting boards are actually health-code violations in some cities).

In a recent development, what we'd leave: Though sanitizing the surface is easy, large rubber boards can be harder to wash because, in addition to being big, they are also heavier than, say, plastic, and the rubber material must be washed by hand. Rubber cutting boards can also hold on to stains more easily than plastic.

In a recent development, in the long run: With its light color this board has shown a bit of staining and evidence of knife blades running across it. But all things considered, it’s cleaned up very well and proven an excellent companion to an always-out end-grain wood board.

Before getting the knives out, we researched chopping boards and narrowed down a selection that included a wide range of plastic, rubber, and various types of wood boards that ranged from about $10 to almost $300.

Industry observers note that to assess the boards’ durability and stability, testers chopped a pound of carrots, diced a large onion, and minced fresh ginger. Testers also cut steamed beets on each board so they could see how much (or how little) each board held on to stains. We chopped lots of garlic on the boards and watched out over the course of the days and weeks of testing for odor retention on the boards. Finally, we washed each board according to the directions and oiled the wood boards that called for it.

Recent findings suggest that here is an example of the kind of staining you can expect with a wood cutting board. A good scrub with some coarse salt and lemon juice will help take care of this.

These are the qualities we looked for in the best cutting boards.

We recommend that home kitchens have one large cutting board, ideally around 20" x 15". Additionally, it’s useful to have some supplemental smaller plastic or wood cutting boards (in the 16" x 12" and 12" x 8" ranges) that are easier to transport to the sink for washing or that fit in the dishwasher. You’ll have your bases covered when you have a large board that can take on any large cooking prep task without risk of vegetables flying all over the kitchen, or upon which you can plop a giant piece of meat for carving—but also some small boards that can be used daily for lighter prep, eliminating the need for a daily full-scale clean of your large board.

During testing, I also looked out for board height; if your board is too tall, it adds too much height to the counter, making it awkward for shorter home cooks to get a good angle when cutting. A too big or too heavy board is also hard to clean and move.

We recommend rubber, wood, and plastic cutting boards. There’s a trade-off involved in selecting the right hardness level for a cutting board. A material that’s too hard will have you busting out your knife sharpener more often than you should, while a board that’s too soft will end up with cut marks so deep you may no longer have a smooth surface—and it will be harder to clean and sanitize. So you want a durable surface that will feel nice to cut on and have some give. For wood cutting boards, we prioritized boards made with American materials. That’s particularly important because wood sourced abroad is often less sustainably sourced, first because it needs to be shipped overseas, and second because the US has more rigorous forestry regulations than some other countries. For a pro-and-con comparison of the various cutting board materials, scroll farther down the page.

In a recent development, if the board had a special feature, like grippers or a juice channel, we evaluated how functional the features actually were. We measured the amount of liquid the juice grooves held and used any prep compartments.

Chop-N-Slice Series Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board, 18" x 12".

Recent findings suggest that if you have your heart set on a Boos Board but don’t have a lot of space or want to spend a lot of money, this reversible board from the John Boos Chop-N-Slice series is a high-quality board with a pretty low price tag. It’s made of durable maple wood and arrives oiled (it only barely held on to stains from steamed beets). It’s only 1.25" thick, which contributes to its low price. Though it’s not too substantial or heavy, it has handle grooves on both ends, which can be helpful if you’re carrying a loaded board. Right out of the box, we felt the board was a little rough, but with a touch of seasoning, it significantly improved.

Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board.

In a recent development, this end-grain cutting board was a joy to chop on thanks to its soft and responsive surface—it genuinely felt the best of any of the wood boards we tested. Chopping feels ergonomic and your knife feels protected. The board is also beautiful and would stand proudly in a permanent place on anyone’s kitchen counter. When it arrived, it felt dry and chalky, so it immediately needed to be oiled and treated, whereas the winning end-grain boards felt more ready to go out of the box. And unlike the Boardsmith and Sonder boards, it doesn’t have a juice groove.

Sources indicate that it also seemed slightly uneven or warped from the beginning: The board wobbled back and forth ever so slightly during rigorous chopping, making a slight clanking noise. This was almost imperceptible, and since we’ve used Boos boards over the years and loved their stability and durability, we think it’s likely the flaw of the particular board we tested. So we’d still absolutely recommend Boos end-grain boards.

Large End Grain Prep Station Acacia Wood Cutting Board.

It has been revealed that this inexpensive end-grain board comes highly recommended by other review sites, and at $72 at the time of writing, it’s an excellent value for an acacia wood board. Its dark color makes it resistant to showing stains, and after being put through its chopping paces, it had no scratches. However, the board did arrive with a visible scratched-up patch on its lower right corner. Even though it was an end-grain board, I didn’t find it as soft or responsive as the Boos above or either of our winning boards. And the wood isn’t sourced domestically. Still, this is a solid value option.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a large and inexpensive board, this 20" x 15" option from TeakHaus is a good choice. The high-quality edge-grain teak looks great, and the darker wood won’t show stains like lighter-colored wood boards do. Cutting felt comfortable, and one side of this reversible board features a juice groove. It’s an inch-and-a-half tall, and that combined with the size makes it pretty bulky. Also, the smell of ginger lingered on this one a bit after we hand-washed it.

This Kickstarter-funded design isn’t just a cutting board; it’s a whole modular prep station. The cutting board has magnetic sides, onto which snap carved wood prep bowls fitted with stainless-steel containers (or silicone liners, depending on which package you opt for). Those bowls also stack nicely on top of the board for storage, and everything can be arranged and rearranged at the cook’s convenience.

Sources indicate that the design here is clever: It’s satisfying to move the board and containers around because everything fits together in a delightful little puzzle, and attaching the prep bowls produces a satisfying click. The magnetic connection is very secure, and it’s helpful and convenient to have little prep bowls available for sweeping away items as you chop them.

You can select various attachable container sizes, and there’s even a large one that runs the whole length of the cutting board that can be used to set up a dredging station for chicken cutlets. You can also buy lids that fit the containers so that they can go right in the fridge to store leftover prepped items, or sauces you made ahead of time for a dinner party.

Recent findings suggest that we like a lot of what’s going on here, but the board’s edge-grain maple construction doesn’t feel high-quality—it was chalky and rough upon arrival. The system is available in a variety of wood types, so maybe the walnut or Brazilian teak that we didn’t test would fare better. But the system is pricey ($519 for a 13-piece set), and the space you’re offered on the actual cutting surface is limited, so there’s not a ton of room for actual chopping—you dedicate a lot of the counter real estate to the attachable containers. If you’ve been in the market for nice prep containers just as much as you have been for a cutting board and love the idea of a smartly designed holistic system, you’ll like the Chef Station. We love the design in theory, but on the merits of the cutting board alone, it’s not a test winner.

Maple Wood Kitchen Basic Cutting Board.

Sources indicate that the JK Adams Maple Wood Basic Cutting Board is made of durable maple. It has a minimal design with no embellishments and won’t add too much height to your prep zone. At just ¾" thick, it’s the thinnest wood board tested. The 17" x 14" footprint also offers a decent amount of space for cutting and chopping but is compact enough to keep in a small kitchen.

The JK Adams Pour Spout Cutting Board stands out because it has a juice groove and a pouring spout on both sides, making it truly reversible for cutting meat. Though this is a sizable board at 20" x 14", the groove and spout do take up a significant portion of the surface area available for cutting, so keep that in mind if you’re looking for something to use for really large cuts of meat. The wood is light-colored and will show stains from something like beets, but keeping it treated with beeswax and mineral oil will provide some stain resistance.

Material Kitchen’s MK Free Board is made entirely of plant-based materials ("100% plant-based biocomposite of natural clay minerals and biodegradable biopolymers," according to Material’s website). That last part is key—especially if you're concerned about microplastics—because this board has none, hence the name. It's dishwasher-safe and has a loop that makes it easy to pull out of a cabinet or hang from a hook. Overall, it’s a totally fine cutting board you can feel very good about using, but without some plant-based bumpers on the bottom, it won’t get a top spot in our rankings. While the microplastic-free material is wonderful in theory, it feels a bit harder on your knives, and because it doesn't have silicone corners, it’s more prone to sliding around on a quartz countertop. And without anything to soften its landing, the thinner, harder material is also fairly loud.

Silicone Cutting Boards Mats, Set of 3.

If you’re looking for a nonporous alternative to plastic, rubber is our first pick. But both natural and synthetic rubber cutting boards are pricey, so you might want to consider a silicone cutting board. It’s key to note that these are mats, not actual boards. But even at ⅛" thick, the material provided a reasonable barrier between the knife and counter. Silicone is flexible so it’s easy to fold into a U-shape to transfer ingredients to a pot or scraps to the trash. These mats are also dishwasher-safe even though they’re very easy to hand-wash. And since the entire mat is silicone, it’s very nonslip. These also have built-in grooves around the entire perimeter and a hole in the corner for hanging and so far, they haven’t held on to any stains (even from steamed beets) or shown any knife marks (even when we tried to make some). That said, some consumers on Amazon have reported knife damage to their mats, which could be a result of the silicone degrading. Though silicone is durable and heat tolerant, repeated exposure to high heat or sudden temperature changes can weaken its structural integrity, and it can hold on to stains.

The All Aboard cutting board from colorful cookware brand Great Jones is like the original Material reBoard’s bigger, curvier cousin. At 16" x 12", it’s significant for a plastic board, and it has a nice loop/handle for hanging. It’s made of BPA-free recycled plastic, and the textured surface is nice to cut on. It doesn't have any sort of silicone grip to keep it in place on the counter when cutting, but it does have a juice groove.

These double-sided boards come in three sizes; one side has a juice groove and the other has an indentation along the top intended to hold Caraway’s tiny Dot & Dash containers. The boards are made from eco-friendly birch, which is lightweight compared to other woods but feels more like maple when cutting. These boards are also pretty thin, so I have concerns about warping, though limiting exposure to moisture can help with that. The board also comes oiled, though it did hold on to some strawberry and beet stains—as we’d expect any wood board to do.

Architec Original Gripper Cutting Board.

Recent findings suggest that this 14" x 11" polypropylene (plastic) cutting board is fine but nothing special. It comes in a variety of fun colors, it has a handle hole you can use to hang it, and it’s dishwasher-safe. One side has small rubber feet (a.k.a. the “nonslip gripper” base), which does keep the board stationary but also makes it so you can only use one side for chopping.

Epicurean Kitchen Series Cutting Board.

As much as we love Epicurean’s multipurpose cooking utensil, the brand’s cutting board is a no-go. There’s much to like; the nonporous wood composite is dishwasher-safe and won’t warp or splinter like wood. Plus, it looks so much nicer than plastic. But one reason it’s so durable is that it’s so hard, which made everyone who tried it worry about their knife blades. It was also very loud to use. The pricier nonslip version (which also has a juice groove) was slightly more pleasant to use, but still not recommended.

At 14.9" x 19.6", this versatile bamboo carving board from Meater (the wireless thermometer brand) offers great surface area. One side is solid and free from embellishments, while the other features a sizable juice groove and pouring spout. But the light-colored wood stained fairly easily in testing and required intense scrubbing after we cut beets on it. And we no longer recommend bamboo cutting boards because the surface is extremely hard on knife edges.

Steelport Steelcore Cutting Board.

The Steelport Steelcore cutting board is a thin, sexy board from the maker of the also sexy Steelport knives. It’s a dual-sided board; one side is thin, perfectly smooth end-grain walnut, and the other is a durable recycled paper composite material. Embedded between the two is a steel core to prevent the board from warping. The surfaces are incredibly smooth, and the composite side has a juice groove, which maintains the modern look of the end-grain side. Unfortunately, the board we received had hairline cracks which, without the steel core, would have probably knocked three corners off of this board. For such a pricey piece of gear, it wasn’t well-packaged for cross-country transit. But the fact that the board stayed fully intact even with three cracked corners is a testament to the strength of the steel core.

Industry observers note that made In’s tableware, cookware, and kitchen tools have a lot of fans at BA, and I wanted to love Made In’s edge-grain Butcher Block. One side is a solid butcher block surface without any grooves or embellishments, while the other features a juice groove. At 17.75" x 11.75", it’s also a nice size for big cuts of meat or to use as a charcuterie board. Unfortunately, even though it’s “steamed for durability” and appeared to come oiled out of the box, the surface really showed marks from the chef’s knife we used in testing, and beet juice seeped into and stained the knife marks.

The Totally Bamboo Kauai bamboo board is totally fine. It looks nice enough, it’s lightweight, and it doesn’t stain as easily as other wood cutting boards. But the surface is harder than comparable boards, and in testing, it slid around quite a bit on the counter. It’s also a little high-maintenance for bamboo; you’re supposed to treat it with a food-grade mineral oil every few days for a month, then re-oil “as needed.”.

Sources indicate that the Angled Board from Material, which is generally available in FSC-certified walnut or carbon wood (the latter is actually stained white oak), would certainly make an attractive addition to a modern kitchen. But in testing we found that the smooth laminate coating shows knife marks quite easily. It was also surprisingly slippery when we were cutting vegetables.

Farberware Nonslip Plastic Cutting Board.

Despite its name, the Farberware Nonslip Cutting Board didn’t stay put on the countertop during testing. On the other hand, though it’s not entirely stable, it is a nice size (14" x 10"), and the plastic construction makes it dishwasher-safe.

Nicole Home Flexible Plastic Cutting Board Mats.

Recent findings suggest that cutting boards (especially plastic ones) have one job, and that is to provide a protective layer between your knife and your counter. These flimsy “cutting board mats” didn’t, well, cut it in that department. They also slid around a lot when we were testing. If pressed, I’d say this type of cutting board (er, mat) could be handy to have around to put on top of a wood cutting board or butcher block countertop to help keep the wood clean and avoid cross-contamination when handling raw meat, but wouldn’t use this for chopping, slicing, or dicing directly on a stone countertop.

The first thing you need to decide on when choosing a cutting board is which material you prefer. Here’s a rundown of what's good and bad about each.

PROS: Plastic cutting boards are useful as a supplement to a larger wooden board because they are lightweight and easy to carry around the kitchen. They are inexpensive, and they can go in the dishwasher. According to food director Chris Morocco, plastic is also a less absorbent material than wood (and about the same as rubber), which means they won’t harbor bacteria as easily. They’re a great choice for cutting raw meat.

Sources indicate that CONS: Plastic boards are harder on your knives than wooden or rubber boards. They will also get dinged up after heavy use, which makes them prone to trapping bacteria. Plastic boards will need to be replaced more often than their wooden counterparts. Some research indicates that microplastics in food could be linked to plastic cutting board use, but the research on the long-term health effects of microplastics remains unclear. You do run the risk of your cutting surface moving around a bit unless you go with one that’s designed to stay put like our top pick here. Chris recommends laying a damp dish towel, paper towel, or nonslip rubber mat under your plastic board to keep it steady. Again, we recommend using your plastic cutting boards supplementally, for less rigorous chopping tasks than your wooden chopping blocks.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: If you’re the kind of home cook who is a dishwasher devotee, isn’t quite ready to invest in a cutting board, or wants to cut up raw chicken one day and mince garlic the next and needs a board that can be a totally clean slate each time, then plastic boards are the pick for you.

PROS: In general, wood is soft enough to protect your chef’s knife but still hard enough for smooth cuts, making it perfect for prepping everything except raw meat, Chris says. (Though you can do that, too, if you’re willing to give them a thorough soapy hand-washing afterward.) Another thing we love about wood boards is that they tend to “heal” themselves (i.e., they close up those knife marks after use), which prevents germ-harboring grooves from forming and keeps them in good shape for longer.

According to recent reports, CONS: These boards require the most maintenance because wood is the most absorbent board material out there. They’re prone to retaining odors and stains, which means cleaning and caring for them is extra important—and requires more work than plastic or rubber. Scroll to the end for more on how to perform that care. We'll also note that an exception to the “easy on knives” rule is teak, which is a dense hardwood containing silica, a substance known to dull blades. So make sure to check which wood your board is made of, especially because teak boards tend to be less expensive.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Wood boards are best for those who care about beautiful objects and are game to give their kitchenware the care and attention it deserves—you know, the people who are regularly sharpening their knives, maintaining the seasoning on their cast-iron pans, and deep-cleaning their Dutch ovens.

In a recent development, end-grain wood vs. Edge-grain wood.

Wood cutting boards come in two styles: edge-grain and end-grain. In edge-grain cutting boards, the wood grains are aligned horizontally. In end-grain boards, the wood fibers are aligned vertically. End-grain boards are easier on your knives, because the knife blade slips between the fibers of the board rather than sliding across them. End-grain boards also self-heal better than edge-grain boards, because the fibers can come back together. End-grain boards dry more rapidly than edge-grain boards because the individual fibers are more exposed to air. This means they require more regular oiling. However, they are also far less likely to crack than edge-grain boards.

It has been revealed that in previous versions of this review, we recommended edge-grain cutting boards because they tend to be less expensive. However, in our most recent enhancement we found plenty of end-grain boards that were within $20 to $30 dollars of their edge-grain competitors. Because the research really highlights that end-grain boards offer better longevity and are better for knife care, we’ve opted to recommend boards only in that style for our top picks this time around. Even if you invest in one that’s expensive (our favorite from Boardsmith), it will last you a very, very with proper care—the cost per use just makes sense.

Rubber cutting boards used to be found only in restaurant supply stores, but they have become more available on the market for regular home cooks in recent years—though they are still as expensive as wood boards.

According to recent reports, PROS: The rubber boards were some of our favorites in testing, because the material is so responsive. It’s lovely to slice on this springy surface. Rubber is soft, so it’s extremely easy on knives. The material is also non-porous, and therefore won’t absorb bacteria easily and is scratch resistant. They tend to have slightly textured surfaces, which is helpful for keeping them steady on the countertop. They’re super durable. While they aren’t usually dishwasher-safe, they don’t need any mineral oil applied (unlike wood cutting boards, which do); just wash them with mild detergent and leave them to air-dry.

Sources indicate that CONS: The only real cons here are that rubber cutting boards don’t have the luxe look and feel you get from a wood board. They also tend to be heavier and pricier than plastic ones.

There’s a reason these boards are so commonly found in sushi restaurants—the bouncy, softer surface supports a slicing motion rather than a rocking motion, making it optimal for ultra thin-bladed Japanese knives. If you like a heavier Western-style knife and use a rocking motion while chopping, this might not be the right board surface for you. Rubber boards are also quite heavy and difficult to maneuver around the kitchen, and they don’t look as nice as wooden boards.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Rubber cutting boards are great for people who like to use Japanese knives and want to invest in a piece of equipment that will last them for years to come, but doesn’t require a whole lot of upkeep.

Cutting board materials we don’t recommend.

How do you clean a plastic cutting board?

It has been revealed that as mentioned above, plastic cutting boards are the most low-maintenance option, as you can simply pop (most of) them in the dishwasher. Though, if you’re cutting meat or fish, you need to scrape off any remnants under cold water before throwing it in. In restaurant kitchens, people often have a metal scraper that looks a bit like a palette knife for this; your stainless-steel bench scraper or plastic pastry scraper can also work. It prevents the proteins from cooking into the board’s nooks and crannies in hot water.

How do you clean a rubber cutting board?

Recent findings suggest that use that same cold water scraping technique if you have a rubber board, then follow with a hot, sudsy soap-up. Both rubber and plastic boards can be left to air-dry because they aren’t prone to warping.

How do you clean a wood cutting board?

Wood cutting boards are a different story than any of the above materials. They’re high-maintenance–but also beautiful, long-lasting, and soft on your chef’s knife. Since you’re using your plastic or rubber board for raw meat (right?), a scrape-down followed by a warm, soapy hand-wash is usually enough for wood boards. Just don’t forget the underside. If you constantly get only one side of the board wet, you are unevenly hydrating the wood. Keep that same idea in mind when cutting: If your board is reversible, try to use both sides of it. If not, chop in different zones of your board to keep the surface evenly worn. That might sound like a lot, but if you chop in the same 2" quadrant daily, the angle on your board will swiftly change, which can cause slippage and, eventually, dull knives. Drying is the last, crucial step. With a clean dish towel, dry your board as thoroughly as possible. Then prop it up on its side until bone-dry to further guard against warping or cracking.

In a recent development, because knife-friendly wood can harbor bacteria and is prone to staining, an occasional sanitizing session is necessary—and if you are using your wood board for meat, those sessions should be more frequent. Sprinkle any stained areas with coarse salt and rub them with the cut side of half a lemon. To disinfect, dilute some white vinegar with water and spray the surface of your board. Let it sit for a couple minutes before washing and drying. If necessary, you can also sanitize your wood board with a bleach solution, but be sure to dry and then oil it really well after.

Industry observers note that POST-CLEANING CARE: Beyond washing, wood boards need to be treated with some TLC. Step right this way for an in-depth explainer on how to clean and care for it, but here’s the gist: At least once a month, pull out a clean microfiber cloth, a food-grade mineral oil, and a food-safe board sealant that combines oil with a protective beeswax. This is just as true if you have an inexpensive teak, acacia wood as it is if you go with something pricier, like a cherry or walnut cutting board.

Rub a small bit of the oil onto every surface of your dry, clean board. (You want the board to be really dry before you do this, so as to not seal in moisture.) Follow with the balm, which will buff into a creamy consistency. Don’t wipe that away just yet. Leave your board to deep-condition overnight, and then in the morning, gently wipe away any extra with a cloth or paper towel.

Gloria Steinem’s Memorial Was a Celebration—and One Big Talking Circle

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1455 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, “Celebrating the glorious life of Gloria.” Those were the words projected against a red backdrop behind the stage at the Park Avenue Armory on Wednesday evening.
  • Sources indicate that the mood was celebratory, which is, according to her friends who organized the occasion, exactly what she wanted.
  • It has been revealed that former first ladies Michelle Obama and Jill Biden were among those front and center, with Meg Ryan, Marisa Tomei, Bette Midler, Diane von Furstenberg, Ashley Judd, Thelma Golden, Lucy Liu, Keri Russell, Candice Bergen, Annie Leibovitz, Anita Hill, Christy Turlington, and Padma Lakshmi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “Celebrating the glorious life of Gloria.” Those were the words projected against a red backdrop behind the stage at the Park Avenue Armory on Wednesday evening. Politicians (some, like Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, newly elected in the midterm Democratic sweep), performers, and poets gathered alongside Gloria Steinem’s family and chosen family to memorialize the pioneering activist, who died in September at 92 years old.

Sources indicate that the mood was celebratory, which is, according to her friends who organized the occasion, exactly what she wanted. That, and no mentions of God, mentioned fellow activist and author Amy Richards, drawing a laugh from the crowd.

It has been revealed that former first ladies Michelle Obama and Jill Biden were among those front and center, with Meg Ryan, Marisa Tomei, Bette Midler, Diane von Furstenberg, Ashley Judd, Thelma Golden, Lucy Liu, Keri Russell, Candice Bergen, Annie Leibovitz, Anita Hill, Christy Turlington, and Padma Lakshmi. Attendees sat in chairs arranged in giant semi-circles to mirror the talking circles Steinem regularly hosted at her Upper East Side apartment (the final one took place with a group of teenagers just three weeks before her death). The guest list reflected Steinem’s wide-ranging reach. “There’s nothing intimidating about this room at all,” quipped producer and philanthropist Abigail Disney.

Sources indicate that the night kicked off with the song “Hold On” by Heidi Wilson, which was written in 2018 after the suicide of a Vermont teenager and went on to be adopted as an anthem of solidarity during more recent protests in Minneapolis and Upcoming York. It was performed by a group dubbed ‘Gloria’s Choir,’ which included the Indigo Girls, actress Emma Watson, Leona Naess, and the members of indie rock band Betty, who have been together since 1986. “Gloria was our favorite rockstar,” remarked Betty bassist Alyson Palmer, beaming.

In a recent development, alice Walker, one of Steinem’s closest friends, couldn’t be there, so Mariska Hargitay took to the stage to read “She,” a poem Walker wrote for Steinem on her 75th birthday: “She is the one whowithout hesitation comes to my aid and my defense. / She is the one who believes my side of the story first. / She is the one whose heart is open. / She is our sister, our teacher, our friend.”.

In a recent development, barbara Lee, the first Black woman mayor of Oakland and Steinem’s friend and collaborator of over 50 years, spoke passionately about their early activist years with Bella Abzug and campaigning for Shirley Chisholm. “When others stepped away, Gloria stepped forward,” she stated.

“Hello everybody, I’m Marlo,” said a glowing Marlo Thomas as she adjusted the mic, as if anyone needed an introduction. It was during her time playing the single, struggling actress Ann Marie on That Girl that she first crossed paths with Steinem. Thomas was approached about playing Steinem on screen and in a meeting for the project the would-be producer looked at the two of them and said, “I don’t know which one of you I want to f*ck first.” The meeting was a bust, of course, Thomas said, but their friendship endured and the two spent countless holidays together. Thomas was at Steinem’s bedside during her final days, reading Native American prayers and Googling the Kaddish so she could recite it to her.

Sources indicate that musician Blake Morgan read a poem by his mother Robin Morgan, the poet, activist, and editor of the seminal feminist anthology Sisterhood Is Powerful, who died a few days after Steinem. Morgan and Steinem, along with three other women, had met monthly for dinner for the past 50 years, and their enduring friendship inspired the words of the poem “Giants at the Corner Table.” “There will be three someday, then two, then one. / That one will carry in herself some of the best of all of us because in each other’s presence some of the best of each of us came forth. / And when she goes, the women we were to one another will all wink out, the work we’ve shared lasting perhaps a little while beyond us.”.

Recent findings suggest that cyndi Lauper, in leather pants and pink-streaked hair, declared that “without Gloria, there wouldn’t have been ‘Girls Just Wanna Have Fun,’” before launching into an acoustic rendition of her most famous song. Obama was the first one in the crowd to stand up and start dancing and singing along, prompting everyone to follow her lead.

In a recent development, chelsea Handler brought laughs—even without ribbing men—and Amanda Gorman gave a captivating recitation of her poem “We Rise.” Cynthia Erivo was initially slated to sing “I Won’t Complain,” but changed course after hearing the speeches to perform “Imagine” instead. “Gloria imagined possibility,” she noted, before giving an electrifying rendition of the John Lennon classic that reflected the night’s message of hope: every attendee was asked to wear a button that said “Hope-aholic.”.

Public-interest lawyer, social justice activist, and founder of the Equal Justice Initiative Bryan Stevenson delivered what might have been the night’s most impassioned tribute to Steinem, using anecdotes from his own upbringing and their longstanding friendship to highlight her feminist and anti-racism stance. “Is there a woman who made you?” he recalled Steinem asking him after he shared a story with her about when he first declared himself a feminist. His grandmother, he said—the daughter of people enslaved in Virginia and his family’s lodestar, who would also live into her nineties, and whom he could still feel hugging him in moments of conflict and challenge. Stevenson said Steinem, like his grandmother, always moved with love, ending with a powerful message that left the audience in tears: “To be free is to do what’s right, and Gloria died a free woman, which is rare, because of how she lived her life.”.

It has been revealed that former senator Hillary Rodham Clinton, with her daughter Chelsea looking on, gave a closing speech that highlighted Steinem’s love of Louisa May Alcott (an image of Little Women hung behind the stage along with other banners that read “Smash the Patriarchy” and “It’s Steinemite!”). Clinton spoke about her admiration for Steinem, which started when she was in college at the height of the women’s movement, and how Steinem’s work paved a path for her own political career. “She helped make it possible for someone like me to run for president, to win a major party nomination and the popular vote… in case you forgot,” Clinton stated, smiling, bringing an uproarious crowd to its feet. Clinton held a torch aloft in her hands as she echoed Steinem’s mission of passing it on to others. “Gloria gave us 92 years of light,” Clinton said, “and all the tools, memories, inspiration, and hope that we need to keep that light burning.”.

Industry observers note that the celebration ended as an all-out party as Kathy Sledge took to the stage, backed by Gloria’s Choir and Lauper, to belt out “We Are Family.” A solemn memorial service, this was not. The audience sang, clapped, danced, and joyfully waved their hands in unison. Fogo Azul, a Upcoming York-based reggae samba drum line of women, transgender, and nonbinary percussionists, appeared to ecstatically escort the crowd out of the massive room. It turns out that the timing of this week’s event was fortuitous: It fell on what would have been the birthday of Steinem’s friend, the late Native American activist Wilma Mankiller (who also wrote the lyrics for one of the night’s musical tributes, an art song for voice and string quartet in the Cherokee language by composer Anjelica Lindsey called “I Want to Be Reincarnated as Gloria Steinem”) and days before a memorial honoring labor leader Dolores Huerta.

Almost everyone who took the stage spoke about the importance not just of preserving Steinem’s memory, but of continuing her work; of carrying on her activism and organizing; of not retreating from her commitment to equality and justice; of why it was necessary to “keep on keeping on,” as Bryan Stevenson phrased it.

“We will not let her work end without her physical presence,” Barbara Lee said. Gloria’s Foundation is already proof of that. The organization continues to raise money to carry on her mission and even preserve her apartment as a refuge for women’s activism and gathering in perpetuity. Steinem may be gone, but this week made clear that her spirit is still very much alive and in capable hands. As Mariska Hargitay said from the stage, “Gloria will always exist in the present tense.”.

Sources indicate that abercrombie & Fitch’s resurgence has been well documented, and the brand shows no signs of slowing down. Alongside its familiar mix of timeless staples, contemporary silhouettes, and archival-inspired pieces, Abercrombie has introduced YPB, or Your Personal Best: a dedicated line of performance apparel designed to bring the same considered approach to the gym as it does to the rest of your wardrobe.

Comprising everything from tees and tanks to shorts and jackets, YPB reflects Abercrombie’s ability to evolve while staying true to its heritage. The collection makes a convincing case for performance wear that goes beyond the usual sea of uninspired basics and head-to-toe Lycra. It’s also versatile enough to seamlessly move from a strenuous workout to the everyday wardrobe rotation. To put the collection through its paces, we’ve styled three looks that show just how far YPB can go.

I am a chronic overheater so my gym outfits always reveal a bit of skin. (It’s also a vanity thing so I can see my muscles at work when I’m getting after it.) This vintage-inspired muscle tank looks like some of the actual vintage tees that I’ve taken a pair of scissors to without a stranger’s set-in stains. I have a lot of hair that gets in my way so headwear is a must when working out. A bandana is a nice throwback to the classic bodybuilder era and unlike a hat, it does a better job at soaking up the sweat so it’s not dripping down my face.

Sources indicate that the standout of this outfit is the shorts. Compression lined, they’re about as long as I’d go for shorts clocking in with a five-inch inseam. They have a discreet pocket in the liner to store my phone, and they're tight enough so my device doesn’t go flying out when I’m doing high knees. Plus, they’re stretchy enough for putting ass to grass on a squat without risking a NSFW tear between the cheeks.

I’ve come to learn that recovery days are not only a blessing but a necessity. But they don’t necessarily mean you have to waste away on the couch all day. My active recovery days involve a lot of walking, and that means my workout shorts make an appearance once again. I can’t deny their comfort factor, and it’s hard to beat a sweater-and-shorts combo, an outfit beloved by my favorite A-listers.

The sweater was a quarter-zip with an elastic waistband for a more streamlined, tailored fit. And if I’m walking a little too briskly, the top easily comes off to reveal a staple graphic tee in my wardrobe.

Finally, I put on some pants! I don’t make it a habit to wear sweatpants out casually, but sometimes the weather calls for it. Hike ‘em up a bit and show off some crisp white socks, a style swerve I saw once and couldn’t help but copy.

According to recent reports, the staple of this outfit is the heavyweight jacket. Its water-resistant lining keeps me dry when the meteorologists get the forecast wrong, and it’s lined to keep me warm as the days get shorter and the nights get longer. The two-way zipper also allows for some extra mobility, and it won’t bunch up when I sit down like so many other parkas.

The thigh-highs, then, evoked the very same boots that many fishermen wear while on the job searching for their catch of the day. But if you think that the dramatic, slightly-cartoony shoes were a gimmick relegated solely to the runway, well, think again. In the same way that people are flocking to the Chanel stores to secure their barefoot sandals, many have been snapping up the rain boots this month, the very moment they hit the shelves.

Sources indicate that it may seem surprising that so many are willing to embrace what is essentially a pantaboot, but Penn said it best: They are to be treated as more of a collector’s item than a day-to-day shoe. Cranberry Crackle Salad

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cranberry crackle salad combines crunchy and creamy textures with sweet and tangy flavors.
  • Recent findings suggest that I live in cranberry country (aka northern Wisconsin), and when fresh cranberries hit store shelves, there’s a good chance you’ll find me in the kitchen baking with them.
  • Crackle salad is a variation on retro fluff salad that combines cream cheese, whipped topping and fruit mix-ins with a crunchy, candied “crackle” topping (made with crushed pretzels, chopped pecans, brown sugar and melted butter).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Cranberry crackle salad combines crunchy and creamy textures with sweet and tangy flavors. It's a retro-style dessert with a hearty dose of seasonal cheer.

Recent findings suggest that I live in cranberry country (aka northern Wisconsin), and when fresh cranberries hit store shelves, there’s a good chance you’ll find me in the kitchen baking with them. One sweet treat that often finds its way onto our holiday brunch menus is a loaf (or three) of cranberry-orange bread. There’s just something so cozy about the combination of tart cranberries and sweet, bright orange juice—the inspiration for this cranberry crackle salad recipe.

Crackle salad is a variation on retro fluff salad that combines cream cheese, whipped topping and fruit mix-ins with a crunchy, candied “crackle” topping (made with crushed pretzels, chopped pecans, brown sugar and melted butter). In this holiday-inspired crackle salad, the cream mixture is flavored with whole-berry cranberry sauce and orange zest. Fresh orange juice in the crackle adds a subtle citrus flavor, too. This recipe makes enough for a small crowd, and is perfect for sharing at a Thanksgiving potluck or as a fun throwback side dish at holiday gatherings.

Preheat the oven to 400°F. Line a 15x10x1-inch rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.

Recent findings suggest that in a large bowl, stir together the broken pretzels, chopped pecans and brown sugar. Stir in the melted butter and orange juice to coat.

Sources indicate that spread the pretzel mixture in an even layer on the prepared baking sheet. Bake it for five to eight minutes or until it’s bubbly. Let it cool completely on the baking sheet before breaking it into pieces.

Editor’s Tip: Keep your eye on the crackle as it bakes; it can easily burn if baked too long.

Recent findings suggest that in a large bowl, beat together the softened cream cheese and vanilla. Stir in the cranberry sauce until it’s combined. Gently fold in the whipped topping until it’s incorporated.

According to recent reports, fold in the orange zest. Cover the bowl and refrigerate the mixture for at least one hour.

Recent findings suggest that just before serving, stir in half of the pretzel mixture. Top the salad with the remaining pretzel mixture to serve. If you like, add sugared cranberries as an additional garnish.

Editor’s Tip: Avoid adding the crunch to the salad too early, as it will soften up over time.

Leftover cranberry crackle salad should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge. It will last for up to three days in the fridge. The crackle will soften over time once added to the salad.

According to recent reports, any extra crackle topping should be stored in an airtight container at room temperature to keep it crunchy. It should keep for up to one week.

It has been revealed that you can make the cream mixture and crackle up to two day in advance. Store the salad and crackle separately, and don’t combine them until just before serving the salad.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to dial up the crunch factor even more, allow the baked crackle to cool thoroughly before using it. This will ensure it has the crunchiest texture.

It has been revealed that fresh cranberries are a great option when they are in season. To make this cranberry crackle salad with fresh cranberries, you’ll need a 12-ounce package of whole cranberries. (You could also use frozen whole cranberries, but they need to thaw first.).

Recent findings suggest that in a food processor or blender, pulse the berries until they’re finely chopped. Pour the berries into a large bowl and stir in 1/2 cup of granulated sugar. Industry observers note that pavlova is essentially a massive meringue that melts in your mouth. We top our version with whipped cream and fresh berries for an airy and fruity bite that will keep you coming back bite after bite. It may look like a complicated dessert made by only the best chefs, but it's surprisingly easy to make! You just need some patience. The key to perfection is drying it out, which requires you to leave it in a (turned-off) oven overnight after it bakes.

If you’re looking for something a bit more festive, check out our Christmas wreath pavlova for a holiday spin on the classic.

According to recent reports, arrange a rack in the center of the oven; preheat to 300°. In a large bowl, beat egg whites with a large pinch of salt on medium-high speed with a handheld mixer (or in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment) until foamy, which should take about one minute.

While beating, slowly add sugar and beat until meringue is thick and glossy, which should take about 7 minutes. Beat in vinegar, cornstarch, and vanilla until well combined.

Recent findings suggest that pile the meringue in the center of a parchment-lined baking sheet. Using a spatula or spoon, spread the mixture into an 8" circle. Make a small well in the center.

Industry observers note that transfer to the oven, and immediately reduce the oven temperature to 250°. Bake the meringue until set but still white, which should take about an hour. Turn off the oven and let the pavlova cool completely in the oven for at least 2 hours and up to overnight. Transfer cooled pavlova to a platter.

Top with whipped cream and berries.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Industry observers note that store the unassembled pavlova in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days, keeping it away from humidity. Once topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit, refrigerate and enjoy within a day, as the meringue will soften over time.

#54402. Hating Turkey Doesn’t Make You Cool

Hating Turkey Doesn’t Make You Cool

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it is fun to be contrarian.
  • Sources indicate that this is all to say that complaining about turkey on Thanksgiving has got to stop.
  • You would think from the way people talk about turkey around Thanksgiving that a flock of the birds came into their house and killed their mother.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it is fun to be contrarian. I admit to the light thrill it gives me to tell people that I hate oat milk, or that I prefer a wet martini. It’s healthy for all of us to have our preferences. But sometimes what should be a matter of personal taste goes viral, amassing an army of haters who make this preference their entire personality. Think back to the great cake vs. pie wars of the 2010s, when anyone who admitted to liking cake was a tasteless rube. This isn’t even about what you like anymore—it’s about the attention that comes with going against the mainstream.

Sources indicate that this is all to say that complaining about turkey on Thanksgiving has got to stop. It is good, and I need people to stop pretending as if it’s not.

You would think from the way people talk about turkey around Thanksgiving that a flock of the birds came into their house and killed their mother. In 2020, Business Insider wrote that turkey isn’t good and you should leave it off your Thanksgiving table. Vox insists the (horrifying) numbers of turkeys wasted every year are in service of “a dry, flavorless bird no one likes,” while Milk Street claims anyone who likes it must be “pretending.” Even this very publication called it “The Major Freaky Chicken.”.

Respectfully, what on earth are you people talking about? Every year I cannot wait for the unveiling of the turkey. It is the ultimate reminder that this isn’t a normal meal because we do not eat turkey on the regular.

Over the years, my family has more often entrusted me with the cooking. We tend to do a version of this Martha Stewart en papillote method and I relish in the work. There is care required to ensure the meat is juicy and golden, and the resulting gravy silky and rich. There is great satisfaction in carrying out the gorgeous centerpiece. There is a subtle butteriness to the meat, and something wilder that even the most factory farmed bird can’t erase. Roasting a chicken is for a Tuesday. Roasting a turkey is for when you have the day off work.

According to recent reports, part of the joy of the turkey, of course, is the leftovers. Turkey congee, turkey pot pie, turkey melts, which will only exist because of Thanksgiving. A feast stretched out, reminding you that abundance does not last for just a day. Do not rob yourself of such plenty.

Obviously, the haters have not stopped millions of turkeys from being served every Thanksgiving. The biggest complaint seems to be that the turkey is never cooked well. And I’ll give you that, with a bigger bird, that you only encounter once a year, it takes planning and effort to ensure the middle doesn’t become a powdery mess while the legs are still raw. But I don’t know, try. There are many things that are tricky to cook that are beloved precisely because of the exhilaration of the challenge, so I don’t know why turkey gets all the heat.

It has been revealed that if you’re here, it means you like to cook, even love it, and there are no shortage of recipes guiding you toward bird nirvana. So put your hobby to good use, get a meat thermometer, and figure it out. Because as much fun as it is to be a hater, it’s even more fun to prove everyone wrong with a feast.

It has been revealed that listen, we all know that stuffing is the best part of Thanksgiving dinner, but because of the butter, eggs, and chicken broth that usually go into classic stuffing, it's a dish that vegans can't always enjoy—until now! We created a stuffing that's so delicious, you might even be convinced to make a few of your other holiday classics into vegan Thanksgiving versions.

Start your stuffing off by preheating the oven to 200° and slicing the bread into roughly 1” cubes. Spread the cubes in a single layer on a large baking sheet and bake for about 20 minutes, until the bread is nice and crisp.

It has been revealed that remove the bread from the oven and turn the temperature up to 350°. Grease a 13” x 9” baking dish with cooking spray and heat oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add onion to the skillet and cook for about 5 minutes until lightly charred in some spots, then add the celery and garlic and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until the celery starts to turn translucent. Pour in the vegetable stock and scrape up any browned bits—this is where all the flavor is. Season with salt and pepper.

Mix the bread cubes and chopped herbs in the vegetable stock mixture until well combined, then transfer to the prepared baking dish.

According to recent reports, cover the dish tightly with aluminum foil and place it in the oven to bake for 40 minutes. Carefully remove the foil and continue baking for another 35 minutes, until the stuffing is golden brown and crisp on top.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Looking for more vegan holiday inspo? Whip up our cauliflower stuffing for a low-carb option, or try out our vegetarian mushroom gravy or vegan mashed potatoes to truly complete your spread!

Any leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. You can also prepare this dish ahead of time, as it’s the kind of dish that we think tastes even better after sitting for a day.

Sources indicate that this pasta is the easiest way to cram an entire head of cabbage into one comforting dinner. The secret? Cooking it in butter over a long, relaxed period of time until it softens into a decadent, caramelized tangle. Paired with spaghetti, heavy cream, and some Dijon mustard and lemon zest to brighten everything up, this dish is a celebration of how versatile cabbage can be. Feel free to top your bowl with lots of fresh dill, or leave it unadorned with nothing more than an extra sprinkle of cheese.

More vegetarian pasta recipes here.

It has been revealed that cook 12 oz. spaghetti in a large pot of boiling generously salted water, stirring occasionally, until very al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid. Set aside.

It has been revealed that melt 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pot over high heat. Add 1 large head of green cabbage (about 3 lb.), cored, thinly sliced, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring often, until cabbage is very tender and browned in spots, 18–25 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup), 1½ cups heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and reserved pasta to cabbage and toss to coat. If sauce is too thick, add pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time, tossing constantly, until glossy. Taste pasta and season with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with finely chopped dill if desired.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

Recent findings suggest that the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s vital that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Sources indicate that preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

According to recent reports, mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

Ina Garten Just Revealed Her Thanksgiving Menu, and the Sides Are Stealing the Show
